title: One decision graph for every agent on the team
label: What deciduous is
text: One decision graph for every agent on the team Deciduous records why the code is the way it is: what was asked, the approaches considered, the one chosen and what it beat, what was changed, and what happened. The graph lives on a server your team runs. Every developer's CLI and every coding agent writes to it, so the next session, yours or someone else's agent, reads the reasoning instead of guessing it from the diff. What runs where Claude Code, OpenCode, any MCP client deciduous CLI (agents, one per worktree/branch) (add, link, remote status, │ pull, watch, serve) │ HTTPS, bearer token │ HTTPS, same token │ /mcp │ /ops, /export, ... ▼ ▼ ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │ deciduous server (deciduous-mcp, Elixir) │ │ one workspace per repository │ └──────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │ ▼ PostgreSQL (the graph) - The server is PostgreSQL plus the deciduous server, normally on a VM behind a TLS proxy. It exposes authenticated MCP over HTTP at /mcp, and /health and /ready for monitoring. One server holds many repositories, each in its own workspace. A running example is the reference install at https://bobbby.online/deciduous-mcp, on a Hetzner VM behind Caddy. - Agents connect to /mcp with a bearer token. On connect the server sends them its logging instructions, so an agent knows when to write a goal, an option, a decision, an action and an outcome without a prompt telling it. - The CLI (deciduous) writes to the same server. A project whose .deciduous/config.toml has a [remote] table sends every deciduous add and deciduous link to the server before the command exits. The SQLite file in .deciduous/ is this machine's cache of the server, not a second graph. One token per server, not per person or per workspace. Anyone holding it can read and write every workspace on that server. Run separate servers for groups that must not see each other's graphs. Architecture covers the trust boundary in full. Where to go next - Your team already has a server: Quickstart. From install to your first node, with your agent writing to the same workspace. - You are the one who runs it: Run a server, a VM with the Docker bundle and a TLS proxy, or the server binary against a managed PostgreSQL. - You are an AI agent told to set up or use deciduous: For agents. - A client other than Claude Code, or a per-project registration: Clients. - No server, one machine, or offline: Local covers a server on your own laptop and the git-only mode where the graph is a file in the repository. Both work; neither is how a team shares a graph. Once connected: the workflow for how a piece of work becomes nodes, teams for many agents on one workspace, and recovery for picking up where the last session stopped.

title: Join your team's graph server
label: Join a server
text: Join your team's graph server You need two things from whoever runs the server: its base URL and its token. With those, five commands connect a repository: remote login stores the token, remote setup --url points the repository at the server, init installs the agent integration, and claude mcp get deciduous confirms your agent talks to the same server as your CLI. Then deciduous remote status says In sync. Everything below was run against deciduous 1.1.0. The examples use https://deciduous.example.com for the server and a repository called my-app; the output is real, captured against a test server, with the URL and home directory swapped in. This page does not cover running a server. For that, see Run a server. 1. Install the CLI sh brew install notactuallytreyanastasio/tap/deciduous macOS, Linux cargo install deciduous --locked anywhere with Rust Or download a binary from the v1.1.0 release: deciduous-darwin-arm64, -darwin-amd64, -linux-arm64, -linux-amd64, deciduous-windows-amd64.exe, and checksums.txt to check them against. sh $ which -a deciduous /opt/homebrew/bin/deciduous $ deciduous --version deciduous 1.1.0 If which -a lists two paths, the first one runs. Remove the stale one rather than installing a third. 2. Get the token Ask the person who runs the server. They read it from the server's settings file, the DECIDUOUS_MCP_TOKEN='...' line in it: .env in the extracted Docker bundle, or ~/.config/deciduous/server/.env for a server the CLI installed. It should reach you through your team's secret manager, not chat. Store it with remote login. It reads one line from stdin, so the token stays out of shell history and the process list, and checks it against the server before writing anything. Pipe it in from wherever you keep it (pbpaste, your secret manager's CLI); if you paste it at the prompt instead, the terminal shows it as you paste. sh $ pbpaste | deciduous remote login --url https://deciduous.example.com Token (read from stdin, not saved to shell history): Token: stored in /Users/you/.config/deciduous/credentials mode 0600, outside every repository A wrong token stores nothing: Error: reached https://deciduous.example.com but the server rejected the token (401). Check DECIDUOUS_MCP_TOKEN. Nothing was stored. (The message names DECIDUOUS_MCP_TOKEN even when the token came from stdin.) One token per machine. The credentials file holds a single token, not one per URL. Logging in to a second server replaces the first server's token, and every repository on this machine then sends the new one. If you work against two servers, set DECIDUOUS_MCP_TOKEN in the environment for one of them; the CLI reads that variable before the file. 3. Point the repository at the server The repository needs at least one commit first. The server ties a workspace to the repository's root commit, so that an unrelated project that happens to share the directory name cannot write into your graph. In a repository with no commit, CLI writes are kept in .deciduous/remote-log.jsonl and deciduous remote push sends them after the first commit. sh $ cd my-app $ deciduous remote setup --url https://deciduous.example.com deciduous remote setup Every project writes its decision graph to a shared server. This connects /Users/you/code/my-app to one: a server on this machine, or one someone else runs. Wrote .deciduous/config.toml [remote] url = https://deciduous.example.com Connected https://deciduous.example.com holds 0 nodes, 0 edges in workspace my-app Unchanged Claude Code already has a deciduous MCP server Done: this project writes to https://deciduous.example.com. Restart Claude Code so it picks up the server; it sends the logging instructions when it connects. It writes this to .deciduous/config.toml, and nothing secret: toml [remote] url = "https://deciduous.example.com" workspace = "my-app" The workspace is the repository directory's name. Every clone and worktree of the repository should use the same one, so commit this file. To choose a different name, deciduous remote init https://deciduous.example.com --workspace . remote setup has no --workspace flag. Without a stored token it stops before writing anything: Error: no token: set DECIDUOUS_MCP_TOKEN or run 'deciduous remote login --url ...' first. A token given only through DECIDUOUS_MCP_TOKEN works for setup but is not stored by it. If setup fails with cannot reach : ... timed out reading response, the server's /health took longer than the CLI's 15 seconds. Run it again; if it keeps happening, tell whoever runs the server. 4. Install the agent integration sh $ deciduous init ... Creating .claude/commands/decision.md ... Creating CLAUDE.md ... Shared graph server Connected https://deciduous.example.com holds 0 nodes, 0 edges in workspace my-app init writes the Claude Code integration (CLAUDE.md, .claude/commands/, .claude/skills/, .claude/settings.json with an update check and a message-board hook) and then checks the server named in [remote]. Use --opencode, --windsurf or --both for other assistants; see Clients. If you ran init first, before remote setup, it has no server to check and asks where the graph lives. In a terminal the menu is: Where should this project's graph live? 1) This machine: the deciduous server as a background service, using PostgreSQL on localhost:5432 as you (answering now) 2) This machine: the server as a background service, using a PostgreSQL you name (any host, port, user, password) 3) This machine, in Docker: a new PostgreSQL and the server in containers 4) A server someone else runs: you need its URL and token Choose 4 to join your team's server; it asks for the URL and then the token. The choices are the same as these flags: 1 is remote setup --local, 2 is --database-url , 3 is --docker-postgres, 4 is --url . If this machine already has a server installed, the menu shows two choices instead: 1) that server, 2) a server someone else runs. Without a terminal (a script, CI, an agent's shell), init writes its files and then stops: Error: /Users/you/code/my-app has no server configured ([remote] in .deciduous/config.toml), and there is no terminal to ask where its graph should live. Choose one: deciduous remote setup --local this machine: a background service, PostgreSQL on localhost:5432 deciduous remote setup --database-url this machine's server, a PostgreSQL you name deciduous remote setup --docker-postgres this machine: PostgreSQL and the server in Docker deciduous remote setup --url a server someone else runs then rerun this command. Tests and CI in a throwaway directory can set DECIDUOUS_NO_SERVER=1. It exits 1. Run step 3, then init again; files that already exist are skipped. init 1.1.0 also sets up the no-server git mode even when [remote] is there: .deciduous/graph.json, a !.deciduous/graph.json line in .gitignore that tracks it, a .gitattributes line and a git merge driver. With a server, the graph is on the server and graph.json is only a local copy that the CLI rewrites on every write; committed, it would conflict between every two developers for nothing. Delete the !.deciduous/graph.json line from .gitignore and leave .gitattributes out of your commits. (deciduous update knows this and skips those files in a project with [remote]; init does not, and running init again puts the line back.) 5. Make sure Claude Code talks to the same server remote setup registers the server with Claude Code (user scope, every repository) only when Claude Code has no server called deciduous yet. If it already has one, setup prints Unchanged Claude Code already has a deciduous MCP server and leaves it alone, even when that one points at a different server. Your CLI writes then go to one graph and your agent's to another, and nothing warns you. Check it: sh $ claude mcp get deciduous deciduous: Scope: User config (available in all your projects) Status: ✔ Connected Type: http URL: https://old-server.example.com/deciduous-mcp/mcp Headers: Authorization: Bearer This is the mismatch the step exists for, and it happened while this page was being written: the project pointed at one server and Claude Code at another. The URL must be your [remote] url followed by /mcp. If it is not, replace the registration: sh claude mcp remove deciduous -s user claude mcp add --scope user --transport http deciduous https://deciduous.example.com/mcp \ --header "Authorization: Bearer $DECIDUOUS_MCP_TOKEN" The shell expands $DECIDUOUS_MCP_TOKEN when the command runs, so the token is stored in ~/.claude.json, outside every repository. A user-scope registration serves every repository on the machine; each tool call names its workspace. To pin one repository to its workspace instead, use a project .mcp.json (Clients). Restart Claude Code after any change. The tools appear as mcp__deciduous__add_node and so on. 6. Write the first node sh $ deciduous add goal "Add rate limiting to the public API" -c 90 \ -p "Add rate limiting to the public API: 100 requests a minute per token" Created node 1 (type: goal, title: Add rate limiting to the public API) [confidence: 90%] [prompt: 68 chars] [branch: main] $ deciduous remote status Remote: https://deciduous.example.com Workspace: my-app Log: 0 write(s) waiting, 0 rejected (/Users/you/code/my-app/.deciduous/remote-log.jsonl) local server nodes 1 1 edges 0 0 In sync: no writes waiting, and every node, edge and document matches field by field. Themes and tags are not sent to the server, so they are not compared. The goal reached the server before add returned. remote status exits 0 when in sync and 1 when anything differs. (The CLI also printed a warning that a 68-character prompt looks like a summary. Goals carry the user's message verbatim.) 7. Your agent writes to the same workspace Open Claude Code in the repository. On connect the server sends the agent its logging instructions: a goal for each request, options when there is more than one way, a decision naming what it beat, actions and outcomes. Ask it to look at the rate-limiting goal and suggest approaches. It finds the goal with query_nodes and writes options under it with add_node, passing workspace: "my-app" and the current branch. Your local copy is now behind, and remote status says exactly how: local server nodes 1 2 edges 0 1 Only on the server (1) option cad0b58d "Token bucket per API token in Redis" Edges only on the server (1) b1710c03 -> cad0b58d (leads_to) Differs: deciduous remote pull takes the server's side. sh $ deciduous remote pull Pulled: my-app <- https://deciduous.example.com fetched 2 nodes, 1 edges, 0 deletion(s) imported 1 new node(s), updated 0, removed 0; imported 1 edge(s), removed 0 $ deciduous nodes ID CHANGE TYPE STATUS TITLE ------------------------------------------------------------------------------ 1 b1710c03 goal pending Add rate limiting to the public API 2 cad0b58d option pending Token bucket per API token in Redis To see writes as they land, from your agent or anyone else's, keep remote watch open in another terminal: sh $ deciduous remote watch Watching: my-app 13:37:13 main option "Fixed window counter in Postgres" If the agent's nodes never show up on the server, it is writing somewhere else: go back to step 5. 8. Commit sh git add .deciduous/config.toml .gitignore CLAUDE.md .claude/ git commit -m "chore: connect to the team's deciduous server" With the graph.json line gone from .gitignore (step 4), git status stays clean after CLI writes; the SQLite cache and graph.json are both ignored. init also wrote .github/workflows/cleanup-decision-graphs.yml, which deletes the graph images deciduous dot --auto puts in PRs; commit it only if you use that. Stage files by name, never git add -A. A teammate who clones the repository runs steps 1, 2 and 5, then deciduous remote pull to fill their local copy. The committed [remote] already names the server and workspace, and the committed integration files mean they do not need init. Next: the workflow for how a piece of work becomes goal, options, decision, actions and outcomes, and teams for several agents on one workspace. When something here does not match what you see, troubleshooting.

title: Connect your coding agents
label: Connect your agents
text: Connect your coding agents Every client connects to the same thing: /mcp over Streamable HTTP, with Authorization: Bearer . What differs is where each client keeps that registration and whether it pins a workspace. The one thing to get right is that the agent's URL, token and workspace match what the CLI uses in .deciduous/config.toml; when they do not, the CLI and the agent write to two different graphs and neither complains. | Value | Where it comes from | Example | | --- | --- | --- | | Base URL | url under [remote] in .deciduous/config.toml | https://deciduous.example.com | | MCP URL | base URL + /mcp | https://deciduous.example.com/mcp | | Token | the server's operator; stored by deciduous remote login | | | Workspace | workspace under [remote] | my-app | | Branch | the current git branch, passed on every write | main | Agents never need database credentials. One token opens every workspace on a server; see Architecture. Claude Code User scope: one registration for every repository This is what deciduous remote setup and deciduous init create when Claude Code has no deciduous server yet: sh claude mcp add --scope user --transport http deciduous https://deciduous.example.com/mcp \ --header "Authorization: Bearer $DECIDUOUS_MCP_TOKEN" No workspace header: each tool call carries workspace, and the server's instructions tell the agent to take it from [remote] in .deciduous/config.toml, or else the repository root's directory name. The shell expands $DECIDUOUS_MCP_TOKEN when the command runs, so the token is written into ~/.claude.json, outside every repository, in plain text. If a deciduous server is already registered, setup leaves it as it is and prints Unchanged Claude Code already has a deciduous MCP server, whatever URL it points at. Check it every time you join a new server: sh $ claude mcp get deciduous deciduous: Scope: User config (available in all your projects) Status: ✔ Connected Type: http URL: https://deciduous.example.com/mcp Headers: Authorization: Bearer If URL is not your [remote] url + /mcp, claude mcp remove deciduous -s user and add it again as above. No MCP server named "deciduous" (exit 1) means nothing is registered; remote setup adds it, or run the add line yourself. Because there is one user-scope registration per machine, every repository on the machine talks to the same server through it. A developer whose repositories live on two different servers needs project registrations for at least one of them. Project scope: .mcp.json, pinned to one workspace A .mcp.json in the repository root is shared with everyone who clones it, holds no secret, and pins the workspace: json { "mcpServers": { "deciduous": { "type": "http", "url": "https://deciduous.example.com/mcp", "headers": { "Authorization": "Bearer ${DECIDUOUS_MCP_TOKEN}", "X-Deciduous-Workspace": "my-app" } } } } Claude Code expands ${DECIDUOUS_MCP_TOKEN} from its own environment when it starts, so the variable must be set in the shell that launches claude; it does not read ~/.config/deciduous/credentials. Claude Code asks you to approve a project server the first time, and when a project server and a user server share a name, project scope takes precedence. (The expansion, the approval and the precedence are Claude Code behaviour, taken from its documentation; this page did not test them.) X-Deciduous-Workspace wins over the workspace argument of every call. Checked against a server: with the header set to my-app, query_nodes({workspace: "some-other-repo"}) returned my-app's nodes. That protects against an agent guessing the wrong workspace. It is not access control: the same token, without the header, reaches every workspace. After either change, restart Claude Code. The tools appear as mcp__deciduous__add_node, mcp__deciduous__query_nodes and so on, 21 of them (MCP tools). OpenCode deciduous init --opencode writes AGENTS.md, opencode.json (which only adds AGENTS.md to the instructions), .opencode/commands/, .opencode/skills/, an update-check plugin, and a custom tool, .opencode/tools/deciduous.ts. That tool runs the deciduous CLI (deciduous add goal ..., deciduous link ...), and in a project with [remote] every CLI write goes to the server before the command exits. So OpenCode writes to the shared graph with no MCP registration at all, as long as remote setup has been run in the repository. To give OpenCode the server's MCP tools as well, register the endpoint as a remote MCP server in its config. OpenCode's documentation (2026-11, its V2 config) shows this shape; it was not run for this page: jsonc { "$schema": "https://opencode.ai/config.json", "instructions": ["AGENTS.md"], "mcp": { "servers": { "deciduous": { "type": "remote", "url": "https://deciduous.example.com/mcp", "oauth": false, "headers": { "Authorization": "Bearer {env:DECIDUOUS_MCP_TOKEN}", "X-Deciduous-Workspace": "my-app" } } } } } OpenCode's syntax for an environment variable is {env:NAME}, not Claude Code's ${NAME}. "oauth": false stops it trying an OAuth login; deciduous only takes the bearer token. Windsurf deciduous init --windsurf writes .windsurf/rules/deciduous.md (the workflow rules), .windsurf/hooks.json with a version-check hook, and, in 1.1.0, the Claude Code files too (CLAUDE.md, .claude/). It does not register an MCP server. Add https://deciduous.example.com/mcp in Windsurf's MCP settings as an HTTP server with the Authorization: Bearer header, in whatever form your Windsurf version takes; Windsurf's MCP documentation now redirects to Devin's, and this page has not tested a Windsurf configuration. Without MCP, the agent can still write through the CLI from its terminal, which reaches the server. Any other MCP client The server speaks Streamable HTTP. A client must: - POST JSON-RPC to /mcp with Authorization: Bearer . - Send Accept: application/json, text/event-stream. - Keep the mcp-session-id header from the initialize response and send it on every later request. This is the handshake, done by hand: sh $ curl -s -D - https://deciduous.example.com/mcp \ -H "Authorization: Bearer $DECIDUOUS_MCP_TOKEN" \ -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \ -H 'Accept: application/json, text/event-stream' \ -d '{"jsonrpc":"2.0","id":1,"method":"initialize","params":{"protocolVersion":"2025-03-26","capabilities":{},"clientInfo":{"name":"probe","version":"0"}}}' ... mcp-session-id: session_GOYlpWIM6imVxCMqh0M= ... The result's serverInfo is {"name": "deciduous-mcp", "version": "1.1.0"}, and its instructions field carries the logging rules the agent should follow (quoted on For agents). A client that shows the instructions to its model gets the workflow without any project file. Codex, Cursor and others take the same URL and headers in their own config format. Their syntax for referencing an environment variable differs per client; keep the token out of any file you commit. Not the same thing: deciduous mcp deciduous mcp is a different MCP server: it runs on stdin/stdout, on the machine, against the local database, with 34 tools under different names (link_nodes, search_nodes, trace_chain, list_nodes, ...). If your agent's tool list has those names, it is talking to this one, not to /mcp. In a project with [remote] its writes do reach the server, the same way CLI writes do (an add_node through it showed up as In sync in remote status). But it sends no instructions on connect, and its tools take local integer ids. Prefer the HTTP endpoint; use deciduous mcp only for a client that cannot speak HTTP, or for the no-server mode on Local. Making the CLI and the agent agree Three settings have to match, and nothing checks that they do: 1. URL. [remote] url + /mcp is the URL in the client's registration (claude mcp get deciduous). 2. Token. The CLI uses $DECIDUOUS_MCP_TOKEN if it is set, otherwise ~/.config/deciduous/credentials (under $XDG_CONFIG_HOME if that is set). The client uses whatever its registration holds. A stale DECIDUOUS_MCP_TOKEN in your shell overrides a fresh remote login. 3. Workspace. [remote] workspace is what the agent passes as workspace, or what the X-Deciduous-Workspace header says. Then prove it in both directions. Write a goal with the CLI and ask the agent to find it with query_nodes; the change_id it reports starts with the CHANGE column deciduous nodes prints. Have the agent write a node and run deciduous remote status: the node is listed under Only on the server, and deciduous remote pull brings it down. If the agent's node is not there, it went to another server or another workspace. list_workspaces on the agent's side shows where. One trap in that check: the two sides use different ids. The CLI shows small local integers and an 8-character change_id prefix; the server's tools use UUIDs. add_node's parent_id must be the server UUID from query_nodes. A change_id is refused: parent_id is not a node id: "b1710c03"

title: For agents: setting up and using deciduous
label: For agents
text: For agents: setting up and using deciduous This page is written to you, the coding agent that was told "set up deciduous here" or "use deciduous". The graph lives on a server the user's team runs; your job is to connect this repository to that server, prove the connection, and then write to the graph while you work. The one thing you must not do is guess which server. Ask. Everything here is true of deciduous 1.1.0. The output shown was captured from it. First, find out what is already there Run these from the repository root and read the results before doing anything else: sh deciduous --version deciduous 1.1.0 git rev-parse --show-toplevel cat .deciduous/config.toml 2>/dev/null look for a [remote] table claude mcp get deciduous Claude Code only; read-only - [remote] with url and workspace is present: the repository is connected. Skip to Verify. - No .deciduous/, or no [remote]: it needs setting up. Ask the user first (next section). - Your tool list has mcp__deciduous__add_node, query_nodes, check_activity: you are connected to a deciduous server over HTTP. It has link_nodes, search_nodes, trace_chain: you are on the local deciduous mcp stdio server instead, which has different tools and sends no logging instructions; tell the user. Ask the user, never invent Before any setup command, ask: 1. Which server? Its base URL, for example https://deciduous.example.com. Do not make one up, do not assume http://127.0.0.1:4000, and do not pick remote setup --local because it needs no answer. --local installs a server and a background service on this machine; that is the user's decision, covered on Local. 2. Is the token already on this machine? It is if ~/.config/deciduous/credentials exists or DECIDUOUS_MCP_TOKEN is set. If not, the user gets it from whoever runs the server and stores it themselves: sh deciduous remote login --url https://deciduous.example.com It reads the token from stdin and checks it against the server before storing it. Never ask the user to paste the token into the conversation, never put it in a file in the repository, a node, or a commit. Do not run remote login or remote logout yourself: there is one stored token per machine, and login replaces it for every repository on the machine. 3. Should the integration files be committed (CLAUDE.md, .claude/), or kept to this checkout? If the user says they have no server and want one, point them at Run a server; do not stand one up unasked. Set up With the URL from the user and the token stored: sh deciduous remote setup --url https://deciduous.example.com deciduous init Order matters. Your shell is not a terminal, and init in a repository with no [remote] cannot ask where the graph lives. It writes its files, then fails: Error: /path/to/my-app has no server configured ([remote] in .deciduous/config.toml), and there is no terminal to ask where its graph should live. Choose one: deciduous remote setup --local this machine: a background service, PostgreSQL on localhost:5432 deciduous remote setup --database-url this machine's server, a PostgreSQL you name deciduous remote setup --docker-postgres this machine: PostgreSQL and the server in Docker deciduous remote setup --url a server someone else runs That is a question for the user, not a menu for you. Run remote setup --url with the URL they gave you, then init again; it skips files that exist. Do not set DECIDUOUS_NO_SERVER=1 to get past it; that exists for throwaway test directories. Use init --opencode, --windsurf or --both if the user runs those assistants (Clients). What can go wrong at this step, by message: | Message | Cause | What to do | | --- | --- | --- | | no token: set DECIDUOUS_MCP_TOKEN or run 'deciduous remote login --url ...' first | No token on this machine | Ask the user to run remote login | | server rejected the token (401) ... Nothing was stored or written. | Wrong token for this server | Tell the user; nothing changed | | cannot reach : ... timed out reading response | /health took over 15 s | Run it once more, then report it | | Warning: the local write succeeded but could not be sent: ... this repository has no commit yet | The server ties a workspace to the repository's root commit | After the user's first commit, deciduous remote push | Claude Code's registration may point elsewhere remote setup registers the server with Claude Code only if no server called deciduous is registered. If one is, it prints Unchanged Claude Code already has a deciduous MCP server and leaves it alone, even when it points at a different server. Compare the URL from claude mcp get deciduous with [remote] url + /mcp. If they differ, your MCP writes and the CLI's go to two different graphs. Do not change the registration yourself; it is the user's machine-wide configuration. Tell them, and give them the fix: sh claude mcp remove deciduous -s user claude mcp add --scope user --transport http deciduous https://deciduous.example.com/mcp \ --header "Authorization: Bearer $DECIDUOUS_MCP_TOKEN" Claude Code loads MCP servers at start. A new or changed registration reaches you only after the user restarts it, so until then you cannot see the tools; say so instead of looking for them. Verify the connection Report each check to the user as pass or fail, with its output. A setup that writes to the wrong place is worse than one that fails. 1. CLI and server agree. $ deciduous remote status Remote: https://deciduous.example.com Workspace: my-app Log: 0 write(s) waiting, 0 rejected (...) local server nodes 1 1 edges 0 0 In sync: no writes waiting, and every node, edge and document matches field by field. Exit 0 is In sync, exit 1 is anything else. 2. Your MCP connection reaches the same server. claude mcp get deciduous shows [remote] url + /mcp, Status: ✔ Connected. 3. Your writes land in this workspace. Write a node with add_node (the goal you are working under as parent_id, if any), then run deciduous remote status. Your node appears under Only on the server: Only on the server (1) option cad0b58d "Token bucket per API token in Redis" Differs: deciduous remote pull takes the server's side. deciduous remote pull brings it into the local copy, and status is In sync again. If your node is not listed, it went to another workspace or another server: list_workspaces shows where. Leave the node; it records that the connection was checked. While you work The server sends you these rules when you connect. They are the rules; the rest of this section only adds detail. > - The user asks for something: a goal, with their message verbatim in prompt. > - You see more than one way to do it: options. You pick one: a decision whose title names what it beat. > - You change code or config: an action. It works or fails: an outcome with the number or the error. > - You learn a fact that changes the plan: an observation. An earlier choice turns out wrong: a revisit. Session start: read before writing. query_nodes with workspace and branch, then ask_graph with the topic of the request. check_activity shows who else has been writing where in the last five minutes. If the work continues an existing goal, put new nodes under it rather than starting a second one. If other agents are working in parallel, read_messages with unanswered_for set to your label. Every write carries workspace and branch. The workspace is workspace under [remote] in .deciduous/config.toml; without one, the repository root's directory name, also from a worktree (a worktree under .claude/worktrees/fix-x belongs to the repository, not to a workspace called fix-x). The branch is the current git branch. If the client sends an X-Deciduous-Workspace header, that wins over your argument. Create and link in one call. add_node with parent_id makes the node and its edge together. parent_id is the server's UUID for the parent, as query_nodes returns it in id; a CLI change_id is refused (parent_id is not a node id: "b1710c03"). Never send add_edge in the same batch as the add_node whose id it needs: the id does not exist yet. To make a retried add_node safe, give it a change_id of your choosing; sending it again returns the node already made. One step, one call. capture_conversation_turn writes a step's goal, observations, decision, action and outcome together, all or nothing; parent_node_id puts it under the goal you are working on. Commits. After a commit, log the action or outcome with commit set to the hash. Do not log your own process: reading files, searching, planning, "starting work". The test: would the user put it in a PR description? When a line of work ends: close_thread writes the closing outcome and can mark the goal completed; then find_orphans and link anything it lists except root goals. Tell the user which nodes you added. Another session writing your branch does not block you. Agents in parallel coordinate on the message board (post_message, read_messages, reply_to), never in a scratch file. Teams has the details. Writing from the CLI instead In a project with [remote], deciduous add and deciduous link write to the server before the command exits, so a shell is a fallback when MCP is not available. CLI node references are local ids or change_id prefixes, not server UUIDs: sh deciduous add goal "Add rate limiting to the public API" -c 90 -p " " deciduous link b1710c03 2 -r "possible approach" The local copy does not see MCP writes until it pulls. Linking the CLI to a node you just made through MCP fails until deciduous remote pull: $ deciduous link 80f8630d 6 -r "implements the decision" Error: No node has a change_id starting with '80f8630d'. Run 'deciduous sync' if a teammate created it. It is not a server id in workspace my-app either. $ deciduous remote pull ... $ deciduous link 80f8630d 6 -r "implements the decision" Created edge 5 (7 -> 6 via leads_to) (With a server, the fix is remote pull, not the sync the message names.) More: the workflow, recovering context, MCP tools, troubleshooting.

title: Record the work as goal, options, decision, action, outcome
label: Record the reasoning
text: Record the work as goal, options, decision, action, outcome A useful graph answers two questions for whoever comes next: what was asked for, and what has already been tried. Write each node at the moment it happens, on the server everyone shares: an agent through the server's MCP tools, a person through the deciduous CLI in a repository whose .deciduous/config.toml has a [remote]. Both land in the same workspace, with the same change_id on every node, so either side can link to what the other wrote. text goal -> option(s) -> decision -> action -> outcome \-> observation (anywhere) The examples use workspace my-app. Everything shown was run against a 1.1.0 server; ids are the ones it returned. The goal: the request, verbatim Put the user's exact words in prompt. A summary loses what the next session needs to know. MCP: javascript add_node({ workspace: "my-app", branch: "agent-api", node_type: "goal", status: "active", title: "Validate create-item requests", prompt: "Add request validation and tests for the create-item endpoint." }) json { "id": "32d05bcb-1b2b-4b7b-b3b8-170a8aa8b7fb", "change_id": "5ca33b18-c27e-4723-9610-3874a592fb7a", "created": true, "status": "active", "message": "Node created successfully" } CLI (the branch is detected from git; --prompt-stdin takes a multi-line message from a heredoc): console $ deciduous add goal "Bound retries for failed requests" -c 90 -p "Stop retrying forever when the upstream API is down." Warning: Prompt is only 52 chars. This looks like a summary, not a full prompt. Created node 1 (type: goal, title: Bound retries for failed requests) [confidence: 90%] [prompt: 52 chars] [branch: main] The warning fires on any prompt under some length; it does not block the write. Nodes default to pending. add_node takes status: "active"; the CLI needs a second command, deciduous status 1 active. Keep credentials out of prompts. Whoever holds the server token can read every prompt in every workspace (see Architecture). Options and the decision The decision is only written once an option is actually chosen. Its title should say what it beat. MCP has one call that writes the decision, its options and the edges in a single transaction: javascript log_decision({ workspace: "my-app", branch: "agent-api", parent_node_id: "32d05bcb-1b2b-4b7b-b3b8-170a8aa8b7fb", title: "Validate at the HTTP boundary, not after the write", rationale: "Reject malformed requests before they reach the service layer.", chosen_option: {title: "Validate at the HTTP boundary", description: "Return 422 with stable field error codes."}, rejected_options: [{title: "Validate after the database write", reason: "The service would receive invalid input and rely on rollback."}] }) json { "decision_id": "d63d2ce0-d91f-406e-9c4f-7253ee438c59", "chosen": {"id": "894c65c3-...", "title": "Validate at the HTTP boundary"}, "rejected": [{"id": "1644a09f-...", "title": "Validate after the database write"}] } Know the shape it writes, because it is not the canonical flow: the edges run goal -> decision, then decision -> option (chosen) and decision -> option (rejected), with each reason as the edge rationale. The decision is created completed, the chosen option completed, the rejected one rejected. capture_conversation_turn does the same for options inside a larger step. Pass the options as objects and mark the winner, or every option is recorded as rejected: javascript options_considered: [{title: "Codes in a shared enum", chosen: true}, {title: "Codes as string literals"}], decision: {title: "Shared enum over string literals", rationale: "Tests import the same enum"} With options_considered: ["RFC 7807 problem+json", "Ad-hoc {error: string}"] (plain strings) both options came back with "chosen": null and both got a rejected edge from the decision, including the one that was picked. The CLI writes one node per command and links them by hand, so it writes the flow in the canonical direction, option -> decision: console $ deciduous add option "Cap the attempt count" -c 70 Created node 2 (type: option, title: Cap the attempt count) [confidence: 70%] [branch: main] $ deciduous add option "Use an overall deadline" -c 80 Created node 3 (type: option, title: Use an overall deadline) [confidence: 80%] [branch: main] $ deciduous link 1 2 -r "possible approach" $ deciduous link 1 3 -r "possible approach" $ deciduous add decision "Use an overall deadline, not an attempt cap" -c 80 -d "A slow attempt can exceed the wait budget under an attempt cap." Created node 4 (type: decision, ...) $ deciduous link 3 4 -t chosen -r "bounds total wait even when attempts are slow" Created edge 3 (3 -> 4 via chosen) $ deciduous link 2 4 -t rejected -r "a slow attempt can exceed the budget" Created edge 4 (2 -> 4 via rejected) The numbers are local ids, valid only in this checkout's cache. To refer to a node someone else wrote, use the 8-character CHANGE column from deciduous nodes or the server's UUID; link, status, show and doc attach accept all three. The action: before you edit MCP: parent_id creates the node and its incoming edge in one transaction. javascript add_node({ workspace: "my-app", branch: "agent-api", node_type: "action", status: "active", title: "Implement request validation at the route boundary", files: ["src/http/items.ts"], parent_id: "d63d2ce0-d91f-406e-9c4f-7253ee438c59", rationale: "Implement the selected boundary" }) Do not send add_node and an add_edge that needs its id in the same batch. The id does not exist yet, and the server says so: text from_node_id is not a node id: "PLACEHOLDER". To link a node you are creating now, pass parent_id to add_node instead; an id must come from a previous answer, not be written ahead of it A non-goal written without parent_id is accepted, and the reply carries suggested_parents: up to five ranked guesses with the signals behind each (same branch, type fit, text similarity, open status). Nothing is linked for you. CLI: console $ deciduous add action "Apply a 30s deadline to the retry loop" -c 85 -f "src/retry.rs,tests/retry.rs" $ deciduous link 4 5 -r "implement the chosen option" --commit takes HEAD, a branch, a tag or a hash prefix and stores the full hash; a rev git cannot resolve is refused. The server cannot see your checkout, so over MCP pass the real hash in commit; it stores whatever string you send. Observations: what changes the plan javascript log_observation({ workspace: "my-app", branch: "agent-tests", title: "Reuse the RFC 7807 shape in fixtures", related_to: "32d05bcb-1b2b-4b7b-b3b8-170a8aa8b7fb", took_from: "183e9e9a-153a-4141-9fb2-8312fe486012", why: "The API side already emits problem+json; fixtures that match it keep the tests honest." }) related_to and took_from take a server UUID or a full change_id. An 8-character prefix is refused over MCP (took_from is not a node id: "9ad1b0b7"), although the CLI accepts one. took_from draws a took_from edge from the source node to the new observation, with why as its rationale; Teams covers it. The outcome: the number or the error javascript close_thread({ workspace: "my-app", branch: "agent-api", parent_node_id: "de6ccf4c-877b-406d-a41a-5474d8c764ec", title: "Invalid requests return 422 with field codes", description: "npm test -- tests/items.test.ts: 8 passed.", success: true, lessons_learned: ["The router already parses JSON before handlers run"] }) success: true writes a completed outcome under the parent; success: false writes a rejected one. Each lessons_learned entry becomes an observation under the outcome; each next_steps entry becomes a new goal. goal_node_id marks that goal completed, so pass it only when the whole goal is done, not when your part is. CLI: console $ deciduous add outcome "Retry loop stops at the deadline" -c 90 -d "cargo test retry: 4 passed" $ deciduous link 5 6 -r "test result" $ deciduous status 6 completed deciduous status accepts pending, active, completed, rejected, superseded, abandoned. Its 1.1.0 --help lists only the first four. One step, one call capture_conversation_turn writes a step's goal, observations, options, decision, action and outcome together, all or nothing, linked to each other and to parent_node_id: javascript capture_conversation_turn({ workspace: "my-app", branch: "agent-api", parent_node_id: "32d05bcb-1b2b-4b7b-b3b8-170a8aa8b7fb", summary: "Chose the error format and wrote it", observations: ["Clients already parse RFC 7807 problem documents"], options_considered: [{title: "RFC 7807 problem+json", chosen: true}, {title: "Ad-hoc {error: string}"}], decision: "Use RFC 7807 problem+json over an ad-hoc error object", action: "Emit problem+json from the validation middleware", outcome: "Validation errors render as problem+json; 3 snapshot tests pass" }) It wrote parent -> observation, parent -> decision, decision -> each option, decision -> action -> outcome. Retries and typos A tool refuses an argument it does not have and names the ones it does, and nothing is written: text add_node has no argument "parent" (did you mean parent_id?). Its arguments are: branch, change_id, commit, confidence, description, edge_type, files, node_type, parent_id, prompt, rationale, status, title, workspace; nothing was written To make a retried add_node safe, give it a change_id (any UUID). The second call with the same one returns the first node, "created": false, and does not duplicate the edge: json { "id": "c2bc238e-...", "created": false, "message": "Node already exists with change_id 11111111-2222-4333-8444-555555555555; nothing new was created (linked under parent_id)" } Changing a node update_node changes title, description, status or metadata. metadata is merged: keys you send are set, a key sent as null is removed, the rest are kept. Sending {"commit": "0123abc"} to an action with branch and files left all three in place. (Older docs said it replaced the map. It does not.) When an approach is abandoned, do not edit the old decision into the new one. Record why and pivot; History shows both the one-command CLI pivot and the MCP calls. Before you stop javascript find_orphans({workspace: "my-app"}) json { "count": 1, "orphans": [{ "id": "e0ff0733-...", "node_type": "observation", "title": "Orphan probe" }] } Link each orphan to its real cause, not to whichever root makes the list empty. suggest_parents: true adds ranked guesses for the first 25. From the CLI, deciduous remote status is the check: it exits 0 and prints In sync when every write reached the server, and exits 1 listing what differs otherwise. Writes are sent before each command exits, so it normally says: console $ deciduous remote status Remote: https://deciduous.example.com Workspace: my-app Log: 0 write(s) waiting, 0 rejected (.../.deciduous/remote-log.jsonl) local server nodes 6 6 edges 6 6 In sync: no writes waiting, and every node, edge and document matches field by field. Themes and tags are not sent to the server, so they are not compared. Nodes an agent wrote over MCP show up as Only on the server until you run deciduous remote pull; that is a stale cache, not lost work. Recovery covers reading the graph back.

title: Many agents, one workspace
label: Many agents, one graph
text: Many agents, one workspace Every agent and every person on a project writes to the same workspace on the same server, each on its own git branch. Nothing locks: two sessions writing one branch both succeed and their nodes interleave. What keeps them from colliding is that each can see the others, through check_activity, the message board, and took_from edges that say whose idea a node built on. One workspace per repository The workspace is workspace under [remote] in .deciduous/config.toml. Commit that file, and every clone and worktree writes to the same graph: toml [remote] url = "https://deciduous.example.com" workspace = "my-app" deciduous init adds a .gitignore that keeps .deciduous/config.toml tracked and ignores the rest of .deciduous/ (the local cache, the write log). The server ties a workspace to the root commit of the repository that first writes to it. A clone shares that root, so it is let in: console $ deciduous remote init https://deciduous.example.com --workspace my-app Remote: https://deciduous.example.com workspace: my-app claim: verified (by this repository's root commit) An unrelated repository that merely has the same directory name is refused, which is what stops two projects called api on one server from writing one graph by accident: console $ deciduous remote init https://deciduous.example.com Error: workspace "my-app" on https://deciduous.example.com belongs to another repository: an unrelated project whose directory is also called my-app (the name is the directory name, lowercased) claimed it first, and this repository shares none of its root commits. ... Nothing was written; the project is unchanged. Naming the workspace explicitly with --workspace is how you say two repositories really should share one graph. The server then answers claim: adopted and accepts writes from both. A repository with no commit yet cannot be checked, so its writes wait in the log until the first commit. Worktrees A worktree whose checkout includes .deciduous/config.toml uses it. One made from a commit before that file existed inherits the main checkout's: console $ git worktree add -b old-wt ../my-app-old HEAD~1 && cd ../my-app-old $ deciduous remote status Remote: https://deciduous.example.com Workspace: my-app From: this worktree's config names no server; its writes go to the main checkout's (.../my-app/.deciduous/config.toml) Each worktree keeps its own local cache (.deciduous/deciduous.db), so a new worktree starts empty: run deciduous remote pull there before deciduous nodes. The server holds one copy; the caches are per directory. Agents need the same name. The server's instructions tell an agent to read workspace from .deciduous/config.toml, and to fall back to the repository root's directory name, not the worktree's. If an agent client could still guess wrong, pin it: an X-Deciduous-Workspace header on the MCP connection overrides the workspace argument on every call (Clients). Branches Pass the real git branch on every MCP write. The server cannot see your checkout. The CLI fills it in from git ([branch: agent-tests]); -b overrides it. Two worktrees for two agents: bash git worktree add -b agent-api ../my-app-api HEAD git worktree add -b agent-tests ../my-app-tests HEAD Worktrees start from the commit you name and do not carry uncommitted changes. check_activity: who is writing where Call it before a burst of writes and after each milestone. javascript check_activity({workspace: "my-app"}) Trimmed, from a workspace with two MCP sessions and the CLI writing: json { "sessions": [ { "session": "GOYltCLK", "client": "docs-work", "branch": "agent-api", "is_you": true, "seconds_ago": 0 }, { "session": "GOYljadZ", "client": "docs-work", "branch": "agent-api", "is_you": false, "seconds_ago": 0 }, { "session": "GOYljadZ", "client": "docs-work", "branch": "agent-tests", "is_you": false, "seconds_ago": 12 }, { "session": "cli:4c3b", "client": "deciduous CLI", "branch": "agent-tests", "is_you": false, "seconds_ago": 29 }, { "session": "cli:4c3b", "client": "deciduous CLI", "branch": null, "is_you": false, "seconds_ago": 18 } ], "active_sessions": 3, "window_seconds": 300, "branches": [ { "branch": "agent-tests", "last_node": { "node_type": "observation", "title": "Reuse the RFC 7807 shape in fixtures", "change_id": "81c332df-..." }, "writers": [ ... ] } ], "branches_total": 3 } What the fields mean, as observed: - sessions is every (session, branch) pair that wrote in the last five minutes, not every running agent. An agent that has only read does not appear. - client is the name the MCP client sent in initialize (docs-work was the probe client that produced this output); the CLI shows as deciduous CLI. - The CLI's session is named after the repository's root commit (cli: plus its first characters), so every clone and worktree of one repository shows as one CLI session. link and status writes record branch: null. - branches lists the latest node on each branch, newest first, writers included, whether or not anyone is writing now. branches (the argument) sets how many, default 20; branches_total says how many exist. Nothing in it is a lock. Until 1.0.8 the server took a ten-second lease per (workspace, branch) and refused a second writer; it stopped one-shot clients from writing after themselves and could not stop the CLI, so it was removed. Two sessions writing agent-api at the same moment both got "Node created and linked". Every write is atomic on its own; log_decision, capture_conversation_turn and close_thread are each one transaction. A server-side lock_scope setting is still accepted and has no effect. Locks never protected source files either. File ownership is the coordinator's job; an action's files list is how one agent shows another what it is about to touch, and query_nodes with file finds what was decided about a path. The message board Agents coordinate here, never in a scratch file: a file has no ids to answer, no way to ask what is waiting for you, and is gone with the worktree. With a [remote], the board lives on the server, per workspace, and the CLI and MCP tools read and write the same one. From the CLI in the tests worktree: console $ deciduous board post --as tests -s "@api is the 422 body stable?" -m "I am asserting code and field, not message. @api confirm the shape." Posted 222, to api The API agent, over MCP: javascript read_messages({workspace: "my-app", unanswered_for: "api"}) json { "messages": [{ "id": 222, "author": "tests", "branch": "agent-tests", "mentions": ["api"], "subject": "@api is the 422 body stable?", "reply_to": null, ... }], "latest_id": 222, "truncated": false } javascript post_message({workspace: "my-app", branch: "agent-api", author: "api", subject: "Re: 422 body", reply_to: 222, body: "Stable: {type, title, errors:[{field, code}]}. @tests codes live in src/errors.ts."}) Back on the CLI, in a different checkout: console $ deciduous board read --unanswered api Nothing addressed to api is waiting for an answer. $ deciduous board read --unanswered tests 223 api -> tests re 222 [agent-api] 2026-11-08T18:36:16.277592Z Re: 422 body | Stable: {type, title, errors:[{field, code}]}. @tests codes live in src/errors.ts. The rules that make this work: - @label anywhere in the subject or body addresses a message. Labels are whatever the agents call themselves; agree on them up front. - A reply (reply_to / --reply-to) is what takes a question off the asker's unanswered list. A new post that answers it in prose does not. - board post needs a label: --as, or DECIDUOUS_AGENT_LABEL in the environment. Without either: Error: who is posting? Pass --as LABEL (or set DECIDUOUS_AGENT_LABEL). - --branch defaults to the current git branch. - Message ids are numbered across the whole server, so they jump. since_id / --since with the last latest_id you saw returns only what is new. - Messages are not graph nodes. They are not in get_graph, not exported, not pulled into the cache. deciduous init installs .claude/hooks/board-mentions.sh as a SessionStart and UserPromptSubmit hook. When DECIDUOUS_AGENT_LABEL is set for the session, it shows that label's unanswered messages at start and anything new on each prompt; without the variable it does nothing. console $ DECIDUOUS_AGENT_LABEL=api .claude/hooks/board-mentions.sh start DECIDUOUS BOARD: messages for @api you have not answered. Answer each with post_message reply_to= , or: deciduous board post --as api --reply-to -s ... -m ... 225 tests -> api [main] 2026-11-08T18:43:12.249771Z @api fixtures moved | tests/fixtures/items/.json now carry the problem+json bodies. Borrowing across branches: took_from When one agent's node changes another's plan, record the borrow as an edge, not just a sentence. A took_from edge runs from the node you took the idea from (any branch) to your node that used it. MCP, in one call: javascript log_observation({ workspace: "my-app", branch: "agent-tests", title: "Reuse the RFC 7807 shape in fixtures", related_to: "32d05bcb-1b2b-4b7b-b3b8-170a8aa8b7fb", took_from: "183e9e9a-153a-4141-9fb2-8312fe486012", why: "The API side already emits problem+json; fixtures that match it keep the tests honest." }) json { "id": "3c2a5b0b-...", "message": "Observation logged", "took_from": { "from_node_id": "183e9e9a-...", "from_change_id": "9ad1b0b7-2c85-4383-b9d9-902411abb3ac", "edge_id": "236548bb-..." } } took_from and related_to take the server UUID or the full change_id. A short prefix is refused: took_from is not a node id: "9ad1b0b7". add_edge and add_node also take edge_type: "took_from". CLI, where a change_id prefix is enough: console $ deciduous link 17365e54 2b787037 -t took_from -r "Tests use the API agent's 422 contract instead of inventing one" Created edge 24 (1 -> 24 via took_from) Taking a decision does not make it right in your context. Say in why what you checked. Watching the workspace live console $ deciduous remote watch --types observation,outcome Watching: my-app 13:37:11 agent-api observation "Watch probe observation" 13:37:11 main outcome "Watch probe outcome" It prints one line per node write from every writer, MCP and CLI alike; the action written in between was filtered out by --types. --branch (repeatable) narrows it, --edges adds edge events, --json prints raw frames. It reconnects with backoff when the connection drops and does not replay what it missed; after a gap, query the graph. --url prints a WebSocket URL with the token in its query string, so keep it out of screenshots and logs. What a coordinator still does Deciduous does not assign tasks, merge branches or run tests. Mark the shared goal completed (close_thread with goal_node_id) only after the branches are integrated and the combined result checked, not when one agent finishes its part.

title: Pick up where the last session stopped
label: Recover context
text: Pick up where the last session stopped A new session starts with nothing but the repository, and the graph on the server holds everything the last one decided. Recovery is reading that graph before writing anything: the goal still open, the decision under it, the last outcome, and anything another agent left on the board for you. An agent does it with the server's MCP tools; a person, or an agent running /recover, does it with the CLI after refreshing the local cache. What the agent is told On connect, the server sends its instructions in the MCP initialize reply. The part about starting: text At the start of a session, read before writing: query_nodes for this branch, ask_graph for the topic. If the work continues an existing goal, attach to it. When a line of work ends: close_thread, then find_orphans. So the first calls of a session look like this: javascript query_nodes({workspace: "my-app", type: "goal", status: "active"}) query_nodes({workspace: "my-app", branch: "agent-api", limit: 30}) ask_graph({workspace: "my-app", question: "why did we change the retry deadline?"}) check_activity({workspace: "my-app"}) read_messages({workspace: "my-app", unanswered_for: "api"}) query_nodes returns summaries, newest first: id, type, status, title, branch, change_id, confidence. No descriptions and no rationale. Follow the ids that matter with show_node, which adds the description, metadata (prompt, files, commit), documents, and every edge in and out with its rationale. ask_graph finds entry nodes by text and then follows the edges the question asks for: "why" follows choices and revisits, "history" or "pivot" follows revisits and superseded nodes. Each result says how it was reached. For that question it returned the superseded action and decision, the observation that killed them, the revisit and the decision that replaced them, and the goal: text action superseded anchor Apply a 30s deadline to the retry loop decision pending anchor Per-caller deadline passed in the request context revisit pending anchor Reconsidering: Use an overall deadline, not an attempt cap observation pending anchor A fixed 30s deadline fails batch jobs that legitimately wait option pending rationale Cap the attempt count decision superseded anchor Use an overall deadline, not an attempt cap goal active anchor Bound retries for failed requests get_ancestors from an unfinished action walks back to the decisions and the goal behind it; get_descendants from a goal shows everything done under it. Two traps: - add_node defaults to pending. A search for status: "active" misses goals nobody activated; query pending too before concluding there is no open goal. - A superseded decision is history, not the plan. Look for the revisit after it. If the work continues an existing goal, attach to it with parent_id. Do not log the original request as a second goal with the same title. From the CLI: refresh the cache, then read The CLI reads the local cache, .deciduous/deciduous.db, which only knows what this checkout wrote or last pulled. Agents writing over MCP never touch it. Check first: console $ deciduous remote status ... local server nodes 6 23 edges 6 22 Only on the server (17) observation 048e98e6 "The router already parses JSON before handlers run" decision 17365e54 "Validate at the HTTP boundary, not after the write" ... Differs: deciduous remote pull takes the server's side. remote status exits 1 when anything differs. Then: console $ deciduous remote pull Pulled: my-app ' -f2 ...) looks for a > the tabular edges output does not contain, so it prints nothing useful. Use find_orphans over MCP. - Step 3, cat git.log | tail -30, reads a file nothing creates. The template on the main branch adds a step that runs deciduous transcript import for sessions the graph does not have yet; 1.1.0 does not ship it. You can run the import yourself (Evidence). Check the graph against the checkout The graph says what someone recorded, not what the code is now: bash git status --short git branch --show-current git log -5 --oneline Match the branch and commit in the node metadata to the checkout. If an outcome says tests passed and the code has changed since, run them again and record the new result under the same action. Leaving a session so the next can recover The next session reads what you wrote, so end with: - close_thread on each line of work, with the command run and its result, or success: false and the error. - find_orphans empty, or each remaining orphan linked to its real cause. - A reply to every board message addressed to you. - From the CLI: deciduous remote status saying In sync. Anything waiting means the server never saw it: deciduous remote push sends it. When the server is down CLI writes still succeed locally, exit 0, and say so: text Created node 2 (type: observation, title: written while server down) [branch: main] Warning: the local write succeeded but the server did not get it: transport error: https://deciduous.example.com/ops: Connection Failed: Connect error: Connection refused (os error 61) 1 write(s) queued in .../.deciduous/remote-log.jsonl. They are sent on the next write, or now with deciduous remote push once the server is reachable. remote status lists them as waiting before it fails on the health check. Once the server answered again, remote pull sent the queued write and remote status said In sync. MCP writes fail outright, since the server is the only place they go. Nothing a teammate cannot see should be described to them as shared. Operating covers backups and restoring the server; a local deciduous backup copies only this machine's cache.

title: Attach the evidence, or derive the graph from it
label: Documents and transcripts
text: Attach the evidence, or derive the graph from it A node is only as good as what backs it. Deciduous has two ways to put evidence next to a claim: attach a file to a node with deciduous doc attach, which in a project with a [remote] uploads the bytes to the server; and deciduous transcript import, which reads a Claude Code session's transcript and writes the goals, actions and outcomes it can prove, each marked with what it rests on. Say what ran Before either, the cheapest evidence is a precise outcome: the command, the count, the commit, and what was not checked. javascript close_thread({ workspace: "my-app", branch: "agent-tests", parent_node_id: " ", title: "Request validation passes 8 integration cases", description: "npm test -- tests/items.test.ts: 8 passed, 0 failed. Browser behaviour not checked.", success: true }) "All tests pass" after running one file is the claim the next agent will wrongly rely on. A files list and a commit on a node are references, not copies: the reader needs the repository to follow them. Documents from the CLI reach the server The server's MCP tools have no upload: 21 tools, none of them attaches a file. Attaching is a CLI command, and agents run it like anyone else. console $ deciduous doc attach 5ee7c7c7 test-output.txt -d "cargo test retry output" Attached document 1 to node 6 (test-output.txt) Description: cargo test retry output $ deciduous remote status | tail -2 In sync: no writes waiting, and every node, edge and document matches field by field. Themes and tags are not sent to the server, so they are not compared. The node can be named by local id, change_id prefix, or server UUID (deciduous doc attach de6ccf4c-877b-... file). The bytes are uploaded to the server, which checks them against their SHA-256, and the attachment is recorded on the node. An agent then sees it in show_node: json "documents": [{ "id": "38c69819-818d-4a4f-906c-1e8c6101b889", "filename": "test-output.txt", "mime_type": "text/plain" }] and anyone with the token can download it: console $ curl -s -i -H "Authorization: Bearer " https://deciduous.example.com/documents/38c69819-818d-4a4f-906c-1e8c6101b889 HTTP/1.1 200 OK cache-control: no-store, private, max-age=0 content-type: text/plain test retry ... ok 4 passed; 0 failed Without the token: 401. An unknown id: 404. get_graph lists the workspace's documents with size, description and node. Older pages said doc attach was local only and that configuring a remote did not upload. That stopped being true; in 1.1.0 the upload happens before the command exits, like every other CLI write. What does not work in 1.1.0: - Documents do not come down. deciduous remote pull in another clone fetched every node and edge and no documents: deciduous doc list there said No documents found., and remote status in that clone still said "every node, edge and document matches", which was not so. Read other people's attachments with show_node and GET /documents/ . - A detached document is still served. deciduous doc detach 3 reached the server: the document disappeared from get_graph. But show_node on its node still listed it, and GET /documents/ still returned its bytes with 200. If you attached a secret, detaching it does not take it off the server. Whoever runs the server has to delete it from the database: Remove a document that should never have been attached. The token grants access to every workspace on the server, documents included (Architecture). Do not attach .env files, credential stores, connection strings, or output you have not read. deciduous doc list, doc show, doc describe, doc open and doc gc operate on this checkout's copy in .deciduous/documents/. Deriving the graph from a transcript Claude Code writes every prompt, edit, command and result of a session to a JSONL file under ~/.claude/projects/ /. deciduous transcript import derives nodes from it: a goal per prompt with the prompt verbatim, actions from edit runs and commits, outcomes from test and build runs with their exit status, and an outcome from the assistant's closing report. Each node carries metadata.evidence.kind: proven (a tool call and its result) or inferred (the assistant said so). What it cannot derive is an option or a decision. Whether one approach was chosen over another is a judgement about prose, so those still have to be logged as they happen. Start with the list and a dry run. transcript list reads the directory for the current project: console $ deciduous transcript list /Users/me/.claude/projects/-Users-me-code-my-app new 6494dc2d 2 prompts 2026-11-08 new 305de803 1 prompts 2026-11-05 $ deciduous transcript import --dry-run 6494dc2d Would import (6494dc2d, 2 prompts) goals 2 · actions 11 · outcomes 4 proven, 1 inferred · observations 0 · edges 17 10 files hashed · 3 subagent runs skipped (their transcripts are separate files) · 15 deciduous MCP writes skipped (already in the graph) It takes a session id (looked up in this project's directory) or a path to a .jsonl. Calls the session already made to deciduous's MCP tools are skipped rather than duplicated. Subagents' transcripts are separate files and are not followed. Actions record a hash of each file they touched; --no-hash skips that. In a directory Claude Code has never run in, transcript list fails with the raw No such file or directory (os error 2) for the directory it expected; pass --dir, or import by path. A real import, into a workspace on the server: console $ deciduous transcript import ~/.claude/projects/ /305de803-....jsonl Imported (305de803, 1 prompts) goals 1 · actions 0 · outcomes 0 proven, 1 inferred · observations 0 · edges 1 1 deciduous MCP writes skipped (already in the graph) root goal 1: deciduous show 1 $ deciduous remote status | tail -2 In sync: no writes waiting, and every node, edge and document matches field by field. The nodes went to the server like any CLI write. On the server, the goal's metadata: json { "branch": "main", "evidence": { "kind": "proven", "source": "transcript", "session": "305de803-...", "uuids": ["fd7edbe1-..."] }, "session": { "id": "305de803-...", "transcript": "/Users/me/.claude/projects/.../305de803-....jsonl", "turns": 1 } } and the outcome's evidence.kind was inferred, from the assistant's report at the end of the turn. The nodes keep the transcript's timestamps (created_at 2026-11-05 for a session from that day), while branch is the current checkout's. Importing the same transcript again changes nothing: text goals 0 · actions 0 · outcomes 0 proven, 0 inferred · observations 0 · edges 0 2 already present · 1 deciduous MCP writes skipped (already in the graph) Read what you are about to share. A goal holds the prompt verbatim and an inferred outcome holds the assistant's report in full; both can contain paths, hostnames and anything pasted into the session, and on a shared server every token holder can read them. Run --dry-run first, and import into a workspace whose readers should see that session. The viewer does not yet show metadata.evidence; deciduous show prints it (Evidence: inferred transcript, session 305de803), and show_node returns it in metadata.

title: Keep the approaches that were abandoned
label: Design history
text: Keep the approaches that were abandoned When an approach turns out wrong, the useful record is not the corrected decision alone but the chain that replaced it: the old decision, the observation that killed it, a revisit, and the new decision, with the old one marked superseded. The same structure serves history reconstructed after the fact from commits. Both end up in the shared workspace, written either with deciduous archaeology from the CLI or node by node over MCP. text old decision --> observation (why it failed) --> revisit --> new decision (superseded) A pivot from the CLI, in one command deciduous archaeology pivot writes the observation, the revisit and the new decision, links them, and supersedes the old node. --dry-run shows it first: console $ deciduous archaeology pivot 0a4240dc \ "A fixed 30s deadline fails batch jobs that legitimately wait minutes" \ "Per-caller deadline passed in the request context" \ -r "One deadline cannot fit interactive and batch callers" -c 75 === PIVOT CREATED === 27 [observation] "A fixed 30s deadline fails batch jobs that legitimately wait minutes" └── linked from 4 "Use an overall deadline, not an attempt cap" 28 [revisit] "Reconsidering: Use an overall deadline, not an attempt cap" └── linked from 27 [observation] 29 [decision] "Per-caller deadline passed in the request context" └── linked from 28 [revisit] Superseded: 4 "Use an overall deadline, not an attempt cap" -> status: superseded Summary: 3 nodes created, 3 edges created, 1 node superseded The first argument takes a local id, change_id prefix or server UUID. All of it reached the server; remote status afterwards listed only nodes other writers had added. The work done under the old decision is history too. archaeology supersede --cascade marks a node and everything below it: console $ deciduous archaeology supersede 29d960e4 --cascade Superseded node 5 "Apply a 30s deadline to the retry loop" Also superseded (cascade): 6 "Retry loop stops at the deadline" Total: 2 node(s) marked superseded --dry-run lists what would change; read it before running the real thing. The same pivot over MCP The server has no pivot tool. Three add_node calls with parent_id, then update_node: javascript add_node({workspace: "my-app", branch: "agent-api", node_type: "observation", title: "Mobile client cannot parse problem+json", description: "iOS 1.x hard-codes {error: string}; 12% of traffic", parent_id: " "}) add_node({workspace: "my-app", branch: "agent-api", node_type: "revisit", title: "Reconsidering the error format", parent_id: " "}) add_node({workspace: "my-app", branch: "agent-api", node_type: "decision", title: "problem+json for v2 clients, legacy body for v1", parent_id: " "}) update_node({workspace: "my-app", branch: "agent-api", node_id: " ", status: "superseded"}) Each call needs the id the previous one returned, so they cannot go in one batch. The CLI reads it back as a pivot once pulled: console $ deciduous remote pull $ deciduous narratives pivots -b agent-api === PIVOTS === (1 found) Pivot 1: [revisit 40] "Reconsidering the error format" Old approach: 8 [decision] "Use RFC 7807 problem+json over an ad-hoc error object" (superseded) Triggered by: 39 [observation] "Mobile client cannot parse problem+json" New approach: 38 [decision] "problem+json for v2 clients, legacy body for v1" ask_graph follows revisits and superseded nodes when the question asks about history or pivots, so "why did we change the retry deadline?" comes back with both the dead decision and its replacement (Recovery). Statuses superseded means replaced by a newer approach; abandoned means tried and dropped with nothing replacing it. deciduous status superseded and abandoned work, although the 1.1.0 status --help lists only pending, active, completed, rejected. Over MCP, update_node takes all six. Query the current state with query_nodes and status: "active", the history with no status filter, or type: "revisit" for the pivots. Reconstructing history from commits For a codebase that was built before anyone logged decisions, the graph can be filled in from git. Pick one bounded question (why retries have a cap, why an endpoint has two response shapes) rather than the whole repository, and read the evidence first: bash git log --oneline -- src/retry.rs git show -- src/retry.rs A commit proves what changed, not why. Record the author's stated reason as such, mark your inference as inference, and say what you did not look at. Record options only where the evidence shows they were considered; alternatives you can think of now are not history. The CLI can backdate a node and tie it to the commit: console $ deciduous add decision "Retry with exponential backoff (historical)" \ -d "Reconstructed from commit message" --date 2024-03-01 --commit Created node 37 (type: decision, ...) [commit: 4c3ba126...] [branch: main] [date: 2024-03-01T00:00:00-05:00] The date reaches the server: query_nodes returned "created_at": "2024-03-01T05:00:00.000000Z" for it. --date takes YYYY-MM-DD, YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM:SS or RFC 3339, read in local time. MCP's add_node has no date argument; an agent reconstructing history puts the date and full hash in the description, or uses the CLI. (An older page said a backdated CLI node stays local. With a [remote] it does not.) deciduous archaeology timeline lists nodes in creation order, so backdated ones sort where they belong: console $ deciduous archaeology timeline -b main === TIMELINE === (11 nodes) 2024-03-01 37 [decision] Retry with exponential backoff (historical) pending 2026-11-08 1 [goal] Bound retries for failed requests active 90% 2026-11-08 4 [decision] Use an overall deadline, not an attempt cap superseded 80% 2026-11-08 27 [observation] A fixed 30s deadline fails batch jobs that legitimately wait minutes pending 2026-11-08 28 [revisit] Reconsidering: Use an overall deadline, not an attempt cap pending 2026-11-08 29 [decision] Per-caller deadline passed in the request context pending 75% It reads the local cache; remote pull first. -t filters by type, -l limits to the most recent N, --json for scripts. Narratives A narrative is the prose version: how one part of the system got the way it is, with its pivots. deciduous narratives init writes .deciduous/narratives.md with one section per active goal to fill in: console $ deciduous narratives init Created .../.deciduous/narratives.md with 2 goal section(s) $ deciduous narratives show Narratives ... Bound retries for failed requests > Node 1 | Status: active Current state: [How it works today] Evolution: 1. [First approach] - [why] 2. PIVOT: [what changed] - [why it changed] 3. [Current approach] - [why this is better] That file is local. It is not sent to the server, and the .gitignore that deciduous init writes ignores everything in .deciduous/ except config.toml and graph.json, so git does not carry it either. Teammates see the graph, not the narrative; put anything they need into nodes, or commit the file somewhere outside .deciduous/ with -o. The commands and skills init installs deciduous init writes .claude/commands/decision-graph.md (/decision-graph: build a graph from commit history, with narratives as the source of truth and commits as evidence) and three instruction files, .claude/skills/pulse.md, narratives.md and archaeology.md, for mapping the current design, writing narratives, and turning them into nodes. All of them drive the CLI (deciduous add, link, status, --date), so in a project with a [remote] what they write reaches the server. Review them before handing them to an agent: /decision-graph assumes the binary is at ~/.cargo/bin/deciduous. Check the result find_orphans finds nodes nothing points at; an empty list says the graph is connected, not that it is true. Have a second agent check the important claims against the commits they cite.

title: Backups, upgrades, tokens
label: Backups, upgrades, tokens
text: Backups, upgrades, tokens There are two things to look after: the PostgreSQL database and the .env file next to it. The server itself holds no state, so if you rebuild it from the same .env against the same database, the graph comes back. Every command on this page was run against a v1.1.0 Docker install on 2026-11-08, with the output shown, except where a section says otherwise. Run the commands from the directory that holds the install's .env and compose.yaml. If your machine has docker-compose rather than the docker compose plugin, use that; the arguments are the same. Back up For the bundled PostgreSQL: bash umask 077 docker compose -f compose.yaml -f compose.local.yaml exec -T db \ pg_dump -U deciduous -d deciduous --format=custom > deciduous-$(date +%F).dump The dump includes document contents (document_blobs), not only the graph. Copy it off the VM, together with .env. Without the token in .env, a restored server is one that no existing client can log in to. For a managed database, use your provider's backups or pg_dump against DATABASE_URL. Prove the backup restores A backup has not been tested until it has been restored. Restore it into a throwaway PostgreSQL with no network access, held in memory: bash docker run -d --name deciduous-restore-check --network none \ -e POSTGRES_USER=deciduous -e POSTGRES_DB=postgres \ -e POSTGRES_HOST_AUTH_METHOD=trust \ --tmpfs /var/lib/postgresql/data postgres:17.11-alpine docker exec deciduous-restore-check pg_isready -U deciduous -d postgres repeat until "accepting connections" docker exec -i deciduous-restore-check pg_restore -U deciduous \ --create --exit-on-error --dbname=postgres . They also need to update the Authorization header in their agent's MCP registration (see Connect your agents), which remote login does not touch. A CLI write made with a rejected token is not lost. It is saved locally, queued, and the command still exits 0 after printing this warning: Warning: the local write succeeded but the server refused it: the server rejected the token (401). Check DECIDUOUS_MCP_TOKEN. 1 write(s) wait in .deciduous/remote-log.jsonl, and every later write will be refused the same way until that is fixed. deciduous remote status lists them. Once the new token is stored, the next write sends the queued one along with it. deciduous remote push sends the queue on its own. Because the exit code is 0, a script cannot tell that the write never reached the server unless it also runs deciduous remote status, which exits 1 while anything is waiting. Remove a document that should never have been attached deciduous doc detach does not take a document off the server. In 1.1.0 the detached document no longer appears in get_graph, but show_node still lists it and GET /documents/ still returns its bytes. To remove a leaked file, delete it from the database.
