Documents are addressed by the SHA-256 of their contents, so hash the same file: bash HASH=$(sha256sum leaked.env | cut -d' ' -f1) docker compose -f compose.yaml -f compose.local.yaml exec -T db \ psql -X -U deciduous -d deciduous -v ON_ERROR_STOP=1 -v h="$HASH" went from 200 to 404, and the attacher's remote status still reported in sync. This deletes the bytes from every workspace that attached the same file, which is what you want for a secret. Two copies remain that the database cannot reach: the attacher's .deciduous/documents/, and every backup taken since the file was attached. Rotate the secret itself as well. Watch what is happening bash docker compose -f compose.yaml -f compose.local.yaml ps docker compose -f compose.yaml -f compose.local.yaml logs --tail=100 server For an external database, leave out -f compose.local.yaml. /health returns 200 whenever the process is running. /ready also checks the database and migrations, and returns 503 until both are fine; point uptime checks at /ready. From any client, deciduous remote watch prints one line for each write to that project's workspace as it lands, from every agent and every CLI: Watching: my-app 13:45:15 main action "Written while watching" When a client and the server disagree deciduous remote status compares one repository's local cache with its workspace on the server. It exits 1 when there is any difference, so a script can use it: local server nodes 3 3 edges 0 0 In sync: no writes waiting, and every node, edge and document matches field by field. Themes and tags are not sent to the server, so they are not compared. deciduous remote pull sends anything waiting, then refreshes the cache from the server. That is the fix for "only on the server". deciduous remote push resends queued writes after an outage. Its repair flags (--seed, --repair, --overwrite-server, --drop-rejected, --retry-rejected, --drop , --overwrite) are for a cache that has drifted in ways no queued write explains. Read deciduous remote push --help before using them: --overwrite replaces the server's copy of every row with yours. Common cases are listed in Troubleshooting. Stop or remove docker compose ... down stops the install and keeps the database volume. down --volumes deletes the database. Do not run it unless that is what you want and you have a dump you have restored.

title: Without a shared server
label: Without a shared server
text: Without a shared server There are two fallbacks for when nobody runs a server you can join. deciduous remote setup --local runs the same server on your own machine as a background service, so the CLI and your agents work exactly as they would against a team server, with one person writing. DECIDUOUS_NO_SERVER=1 deciduous init skips the server entirely and shares the graph through a git-tracked .deciduous/graph.json. Use the first if you might join a team later; use the second only when a running service is not an option. A server on this machine remote setup --local looks for a server this machine already has, and installs one if there is none. On a machine that has one, it reuses it and changes nothing about it: text $ deciduous remote setup --local deciduous remote setup Every project writes its decision graph to a shared server. This connects /home/you/code/my-app to one: a server on this machine, or one someone else runs. Found local server at http://127.0.0.1:4000 Wrote .deciduous/config.toml [remote] url = http://127.0.0.1:4000 Connected http://127.0.0.1:4000 holds 0 nodes, 0 edges in workspace my-app Unchanged Claude Code already has a deciduous MCP server Done: this project writes to http://127.0.0.1:4000. Restart Claude Code so it picks up the server; it sends the logging instructions when it connects. "This machine has a server" means ~/.config/deciduous/server/.env exists. That settings file is authoritative once written: every later --local, in every project, points at the server it describes. The flags that choose how a new server is built do not replace an existing one. --docker on a machine with a native server is refused: text Error: this machine's server is already set up to run as a background service (/Users/you/.config/deciduous/server/.env), and it is kept that way. To replace it, stop it and move that file away first; its database is not touched. and --database-url against the same native server is accepted but ignored, with one line saying so: Using the server already set up in ~/.config/deciduous/server/.env; its database and port stand. The Unchanged Claude Code already has a deciduous MCP server line deserves a second look. remote setup registers its server with Claude Code at user scope only when no deciduous server is registered there. If one is, it is left alone even when it points somewhere else, and the "Restart Claude Code" advice below it will not fix that. Check with claude mcp get deciduous; the Claude Code section of Connect your agents has the fix. What a fresh install does The output above was observed on a machine that already had a server. The steps below are what src/server.rs, src/local_server.rs and deciduous_mcp/DEPLOY.md say happens on a machine without one; they were read, not run. | Flag | Server runs as | Database | | --- | --- | --- | | --local (nothing else) | the release's single-file deciduous-mcp executable, as a user service | PostgreSQL on localhost:5432 as $USER, no password, database deciduous | | --database-url | the same user service | the PostgreSQL you name | | --docker | a container from the release's deciduous-mcp-docker.tar.gz | the PostgreSQL from the first two rows; localhost is rewritten to host.docker.internal | | --docker-postgres | a container (implies --docker) | a new PostgreSQL 17 container | | --port | any of the above | used only on first setup; asked otherwise, with a free port in 20000-32767 suggested | With no flags and a terminal, remote setup asks the same questions as a menu. Without a terminal and without --local or --url, it stops and prints the four scripted forms. The native install, in order: 1. Downloads deciduous-mcp- - for the CLI's own version, checks it against the release's checksums.txt, and installs it as ~/.config/deciduous/server/bin/deciduous-mcp. 2. Picks the bearer token. If the machine already has one (DECIDUOUS_MCP_TOKEN, else ~/.config/deciduous/credentials) of at least 32 bytes, that becomes the server's token; otherwise 64 random hex digits. 3. Runs the executable once with DECIDUOUS_MCP_COMMAND=prepare-database: it connects, creates the database if missing (the role needs CREATEDB), migrates, and exits. A refusal comes back in PostgreSQL's words (role "x" does not exist, password authentication failed). If nothing listens on 5432 at all, setup says so and prints brew install postgresql@17 && brew services start postgresql@17 / sudo apt install postgresql. 4. Writes ~/.config/deciduous/server/.env, mode 600. This machine's file has these keys (values other than the secrets shown): text DECIDUOUS_SERVER_MODE=native DECIDUOUS_SERVER_VERSION=1.1.0 DECIDUOUS_BIND_ADDRESS=127.0.0.1 DECIDUOUS_PORT=4000 DECIDUOUS_MCP_TOKEN=' ' DATABASE_URL=' ' DB_SSL=false DB_SSL_VERIFY=full DB_SSL_CA_FILE= POOL_SIZE=10 DECIDUOUS_PREPARE_DATABASE=true 5. Installs a user service that starts at login and restarts on exit: a LaunchAgent dev.deciduous.server at ~/Library/LaunchAgents/dev.deciduous.server.plist on macOS, a systemd user unit deciduous-server.service on Linux. The service definition carries only paths; the token and database URL stay in .env, which the server reads itself through DECIDUOUS_ENV_FILE. Output goes to ~/.config/deciduous/server/logs/server.log. On Linux, user services stop at logout unless you run loginctl enable-linger $USER. 6. Waits for /ready, then stores the token in ~/.config/deciduous/credentials if it differs from the one there, writes [remote], and registers with Claude Code as above. The server binds 127.0.0.1 because DECIDUOUS_BIND_ADDRESS says so; a server started by hand without that setting listens on every interface. Every start re-runs the migrations (DECIDUOUS_PREPARE_DATABASE=true), and deciduous update in a project that writes to this server replaces an older executable and restarts the service. Docker installs are not upgraded by update. A database URL may carry ?sslmode=. The CLI maps it onto the server's TLS settings: require → DB_SSL=true DB_SSL_VERIFY=none, verify-ca → ca, verify-full → full. disable, allow and prefer all turn TLS off; prefer does not mean "try TLS" here. Any other query parameter is refused rather than dropped. The meaning of each mode is on Architecture. The first log lines after a start say what the server is doing. From this machine's server.log: text [info] Database TLS: off (DB_SSL unset or false) [info] Events.Listener: listening on graph_events [info] Running DeciduousMcp.Web.Router with Bandit 1.13.1 at 127.0.0.1:4000 (http) To remove a native install (from DEPLOY.md; the database is left in PostgreSQL): bash launchctl bootout gui/$(id -u)/dev.deciduous.server macOS rm ~/Library/LaunchAgents/dev.deciduous.server.plist systemctl --user disable --now deciduous-server.service Linux rm -r ~/.config/deciduous/server One token per machine The CLI keeps exactly one stored token, in ~/.config/deciduous/credentials, not one per server URL. If you write to a local server for some projects and to a team server for others, only one of them can use the stored token. Two things replace it without asking: - deciduous remote login --url https://deciduous.example.com stores the team token over the local one. - deciduous remote setup --local stores the local server's token over whatever is there, whenever they differ. The other server's projects then fail on every write. The write itself still succeeds locally and the command exits 0; the op waits in the log: text Created node 6 (type: observation, title: written with the other server's token) [branch: main] Warning: the local write succeeded but the server refused it: the server rejected the token (401). Check DECIDUOUS_MCP_TOKEN. 1 write(s) wait in /home/you/code/my-app/.deciduous/remote-log.jsonl, and every later write will be refused the same way until that is fixed. deciduous remote status lists them. DECIDUOUS_MCP_TOKEN is read before the stored file, so the working arrangement is: store the token you use most, and export the other one in the environment of the projects that need it (a per-directory env tool such as direnv, or a wrapper script). Once the right token is in place, deciduous remote push sends what waited. The ordering also matters the first time. A brand-new local server adopts whatever token the machine already holds (step 2 above), so installing a local server after remote login to a team server gives the local server the team's token. Both then accept the same secret, and rotating the team token later breaks the local server's projects too. Run remote setup --local with DECIDUOUS_MCP_TOKEN unset and the credentials file empty if you want the two kept apart. (This ordering was read from machine_token() in src/server.rs, not run.) Claude Code has the same shape of problem: one user-scope deciduous entry. For a second server, add a project-scoped .mcp.json in the repositories that use it; see Connect your agents. No server at all deciduous init will not finish without a server. In a terminal it asks; without one it prints the four remote setup forms and exits 1. To opt out, say so: text $ DECIDUOUS_NO_SERVER=1 deciduous init Creating .gitignore (track .deciduous/graph.json, ignore the database) Creating .gitattributes (merge the graph file record by record, fold it in PR diffs) Configured git merge driver for graph records Creating .deciduous/graph.json (run deciduous sync to fill it, then commit it) ... Skipped shared graph server (DECIDUOUS_NO_SERVER is set) The ignore rules keep the database private and track two files: text .gitignore .deciduous/ !.deciduous/config.toml !.deciduous/graph.json .gitattributes .deciduous/graph.json merge=deciduous linguist-generated=true and the merge driver goes into .git/config, which git never shares: text merge.deciduous.name deciduous decision graph record merge.deciduous.driver deciduous merge-record %O %A %B Every write goes to the local database and is mirrored into graph.json at once. Each write also says where it went, so nobody mistakes this mode for a shared one: text Note: written to /home/you/code/my-app/.deciduous/deciduous.db only; this project has no shared server. deciduous remote setup connects one. Two clones, one graph This was run with a bare origin and two clones, a and b. In a: add a goal, deciduous sync, commit .gitignore .gitattributes .deciduous/config.toml .deciduous/graph.json by name, push. A fresh clone b sees the goal immediately (the database follows graph.json on the next command), but its .git/config has no merge driver until something registers it. deciduous sync does: text $ deciduous sync Configured git merge driver for the graph file (this clone) Synced /home/you/code/b/.deciduous/graph.json (1 nodes, 0 edges, 0 themes, 0 tags on disk) Database and records already agree Then both clones changed the graph at once. a added an option, linked it, and set the goal active; b added a different option, linked it, and replaced the goal's prompt. Both committed; a pushed; b pulled: text $ git pull --no-edit origin HEAD Merge made by the 'ort' strategy. .deciduous/graph.json | 24 +++++++++++++++++++++++- $ deciduous nodes ID CHANGE TYPE STATUS TITLE 1 94e4b9f7 goal active Shared goal 3 d04a258b option pending Option from A 2 01ed84dd option pending Option from B No conflict markers, both new options and both edges, and node 1 carries a's status and b's prompt. The driver merges record by record, and a record both sides changed field by field, breaking ties on updated_at. Deletes are tombstones, so a delete reaches clones that already had the node. A file that does end up with conflict markers (merged in a clone with no driver registered) is repaired by the next deciduous sync. The routine: bash git pull deciduous sync takes in what the pull brought, registers the driver if missing deciduous sync --check before pushing: reports what sync would change, writes nothing git add .deciduous/graph.json sync --help says --check exits 1 when anything is pending. In the one pending case provoked here (the database edited behind the file), it printed Changes would: 1 nodes set back to graph.json's version and exited 0, so read its output rather than relying on the exit status in a hook. Ordinary writes are mirrored into the file as they happen, so in day-to-day use there is rarely anything pending. Numeric ids are per clone (b numbered "Option from B" 2, a numbered "Option from A" 2). Refer to nodes across machines by change_id prefix: deciduous link 94e4b9f7 01ed84dd. What this mode does not have: agents writing over MCP (there is no HTTP server; deciduous mcp over stdio works against the local database, see MCP tools), check_activity, live remote watch, and anything faster than a git push. graph.json also carries every prompt and description you write, so treat it like any other committed file. Moving to a server later Point the project at a server with deciduous remote init https://deciduous.example.com --workspace my-app (or remote setup --url, or --local). The history written before the project had a remote goes up with it. From a clone of the two-clone repository above, pointed at an empty workspace: text $ deciduous remote init http://127.0.0.1:4000 --workspace docsref-seed2 Remote: http://127.0.0.1:4000 workspace: docsref-seed2 claim: claimed (by this repository's root commit) server holds 0 nodes, 0 edges, 0 documents sent 2 local node(s), 1 edge(s) the server lacked deciduous remote status then says In sync. If it ever lists rows as "only here" that no op covers, deciduous remote push --seed sends them; it adds what the server lacks and never changes a row the server already has. Operating a server covers the other push flags. Once a project has a [remote], deciduous sync is no longer the step that shares anything.

title: Troubleshooting
label: Troubleshooting
text: Troubleshooting Most problems are one of four things: the CLI and the agent are talking to different servers, the token in use belongs to a different server, the workspace name collides with another repository, or the server was unreachable and writes are waiting. Each entry below starts from the exact text deciduous 1.1.0 prints, captured by provoking it. Two commands answer most questions: bash deciduous remote status this copy vs the server: waiting writes, rejected writes, rows that differ claude mcp get deciduous where Claude Code's agent is actually writing remote status exits 0 only when it prints In sync; anything waiting, rejected or different exits 1. Setting up init stops with "no terminal to ask" text Error: /home/you/code/my-app has no server configured ([remote] in .deciduous/config.toml), and there is no terminal to ask where its graph should live. Choose one: deciduous remote setup --local this machine: a background service, PostgreSQL on localhost:5432 deciduous remote setup --database-url this machine's server, a PostgreSQL you name deciduous remote setup --docker-postgres this machine: PostgreSQL and the server in Docker deciduous remote setup --url a server someone else runs then rerun this command. Tests and CI in a throwaway directory can set DECIDUOUS_NO_SERVER=1. Cause. init was run from a script, an agent's shell, or anything else without a terminal on stdin, in a project with no [remote]. It exits 1, but it has already written .claude/, CLAUDE.md, .deciduous/, .gitignore and .gitattributes before stopping, so the directory looks initialized. Fix. Run the remote setup form that fits, then deciduous init again. To join a team server: DECIDUOUS_MCP_TOKEN= deciduous remote setup --url https://deciduous.example.com. DECIDUOUS_NO_SERVER=1 is for throwaway directories; it gives a project with no server at all (see Without a shared server). "the server rejected the token (401)" text Error: reached https://deciduous.example.com but the server rejected the token (401). Check DECIDUOUS_MCP_TOKEN. Nothing was stored or written. remote init says the same with Nothing was written; the project is unchanged. Both exit 1 and change nothing. Causes, in the order worth checking: 1. The URL ends in /mcp. The CLI wants the base URL; the agent wants /mcp. Given .../mcp, the CLI asks for .../mcp/health, which is behind authentication, and reports a token problem that is really a path problem: text Error: cannot reach http://127.0.0.1:4000/mcp: the server rejected the token (401). Check DECIDUOUS_MCP_TOKEN. Drop the /mcp. 2. A stale DECIDUOUS_MCP_TOKEN in this shell. The environment wins over the stored token. env | grep DECIDUOUS_MCP_TOKEN, then unset it or correct it. 3. The stored token belongs to another server. There is one stored token per machine, not one per URL. The message says "Check DECIDUOUS_MCP_TOKEN" even when the token came from ~/.config/deciduous/credentials. See One token per machine. 4. The token is wrong. Ask whoever runs the server. (remote login --url also says "Check DECIDUOUS_MCP_TOKEN" when the bad token came from stdin.) deciduous remote login --url https://deciduous.example.com reads a token from stdin, checks it against that server, and only then stores it (mode 0600). "cannot reach ... Connection refused" text Error: cannot reach http://127.0.0.1:9: transport error: http://127.0.0.1:9/health: Connection Failed: Connect error: Connection refused (os error 61) Nothing listens at that address and port. For a team server, check the URL with whoever runs it and curl https://deciduous.example.com/health (it answers ok without a token). For this machine's server, the port is DECIDUOUS_PORT in ~/.config/deciduous/server/.env and the log is ~/.config/deciduous/server/logs/server.log. A name that does not resolve fails the same way, with Dns Failed: resolve dns name 'deciduous.invalid:443': failed to lookup address information. "no such endpoint (404)" text Error: cannot reach http://127.0.0.1:4000/deciduous-mcp: no such endpoint (404). Is the URL right, including any path prefix? The host answered but not at that path. A server behind a reverse proxy usually lives under a prefix (the reference deployment is https://bobbby.online/deciduous-mcp); a server reached directly has none. The base URL is whatever /health answers ok on. "timed out reading response" The CLI gives /health 15 seconds. A server that is up but slow to answer (one production server took 2-7 s per /health on 2026-11-08) can push remote setup --url over that, and it fails with timed out reading response before anything is stored. Run it again. If it keeps happening, the proxy or the server is struggling; curl -w '%{time_total}\n' https://deciduous.example.com/health shows by how much. "no token for the shared graph" text Error: no token for the shared graph. Store one (kept outside every repository, mode 0600): deciduous remote login or set DECIDUOUS_MCP_TOKEN for a one-off. Neither DECIDUOUS_MCP_TOKEN nor ~/.config/deciduous/credentials holds a token. Note that remote setup --url with a token only in the environment does not store it: the next shell without the variable gets this message. deciduous remote login --url stores it. "invalid workspace name" text Error: the server returned 422: invalid workspace name "a/b": it looks like a path; pass the repo root's basename Workspace names are one path segment. The server trims and lowercases them (--workspace "My App" is stored as my app), so two spellings that differ only in case are one workspace. Writing "the local write succeeded but the server did not get it" text Created node 1 (type: goal, title: Written while the server is down) [confidence: 70%] [branch: main] Warning: the local write succeeded but the server did not get it: transport error: http://127.0.0.1:9/ops: Connection Failed: Connect error: Connection refused (os error 61) 1 write(s) queued in /home/you/code/my-app/.deciduous/remote-log.jsonl. They are sent on the next write, or now with deciduous remote push once the server is reachable. Cause. The server was unreachable (or took longer than the 10 seconds a write waits for it). Nothing is lost: the write is in the local database and the op is in .deciduous/remote-log.jsonl. The command exits 0. What to do. Usually nothing. The next CLI write that reaches the server sends everything queued before it. To see what is waiting: text $ deciduous remote status Log: 3 write(s) waiting, 0 rejected (/home/you/code/my-app/.deciduous/remote-log.jsonl) waiting f7b164cd create goal f50e03ed "Written while the server is down" waiting 87b844eb create action 316bf956 "Second" waiting d8aa0105 link f50e03ed -> 316bf956 (leads_to) Error: cannot reach http://127.0.0.1:9: ... remote push while the server is still down exits 1 and keeps everything (3 write(s) still waiting in ...). Once it is back: text $ deciduous remote push Pushed 3 op(s) to my-app: 3 applied, 0 already there, 0 rejected Pushing twice is safe; the server applies each op at most once, by its id, and reports repeats as "already there". For a server that is up but slow, DECIDUOUS_OPS_TIMEOUT= raises the 120-second limit on each remote push request. "the server refused it: the server rejected the token (401)" text Warning: the local write succeeded but the server refused it: the server rejected the token (401). Check DECIDUOUS_MCP_TOKEN. 1 write(s) wait in /home/you/code/my-app/.deciduous/remote-log.jsonl, and every later write will be refused the same way until that is fixed. deciduous remote status lists them. The project's server is up but the token in use is not its token: almost always the one-token-per-machine problem after remote login or remote setup --local for a different server. The write exits 0, so a script will not notice. Put the right token in place (One token per machine), then deciduous remote push. "belongs to another repository" text Warning: the local write succeeded but the server refused it: workspace "p5" on http://127.0.0.1:4000 belongs to another repository: an unrelated project whose directory is also called p5 (the name is the directory name, lowercased) claimed it first, and this repository shares none of its root commits. Give this project its own workspace: deciduous remote init http://127.0.0.1:4000 --workspace or, if the two repositories really should write one graph, say so by naming it: deciduous remote init http://127.0.0.1:4000 --workspace p5 Cause. The default workspace is the repository's directory name. The server ties a workspace to the root commits of the first repository that writes to it, and refuses one that shares none. Two unrelated projects both called api collide here; two clones or worktrees of one repository never do. Fix. Pick a distinct name with --workspace, then deciduous remote push to send what waited. Naming an existing workspace explicitly is how you say two repositories should share it: remote init then reports claim: adopted. A repository with no commit yet cannot be tied to anything. remote init warns, and writes wait in the log until the first commit: text note: this repository has no commit yet, so the server cannot tie workspace "my-app" to it, and an unrelated repository also called my-app could later claim the workspace with these writes in it. Nothing is sent until the first commit; the writes wait in the log, and the first command after that commit sends them. Rejected writes remote status lists ops the server refused (as opposed to ops it never received) with the server's reason. They stay in the log until you decide: deciduous remote push --retry-rejected after fixing the cause, --drop-rejected to discard them all, or --drop for one. None was provoked for this page; the flags are from remote push --help. "Local only: no remote configured" text $ deciduous remote status Local only: no remote configured for this project. deciduous remote init status exits 0 here; push, pull and watch print Error: no remote configured for this project. and exit 1. The project was initialized with DECIDUOUS_NO_SERVER=1, or .deciduous/config.toml lost its [remote] table. A linked git worktree with no [remote] of its own uses its main checkout's. CLI and agent disagree The agent's nodes are not in deciduous nodes, or yours are not in the agent's First, claude mcp get deciduous, and compare its URL with [remote] url in .deciduous/config.toml: text $ claude mcp get deciduous deciduous: Scope: User config (available in all your projects) Status: ✔ Connected Type: http URL: https://bobbby.online/deciduous-mcp/mcp Headers: Authorization: Bearer That is from a machine whose projects point at http://127.0.0.1:4000: CLI writes go to one server, the agent's to another, and both report success. remote setup does not fix this. It registers Claude Code only when no deciduous server is registered, and otherwise prints Unchanged Claude Code already has a deciduous MCP server whatever URL that one has. Re-register it yourself, or give the repository its own .mcp.json; both are on Connect your agents. Second, if the URLs agree: CLI reads (nodes, show, serve) come from the local database, which is a cache. It does not refresh itself. After an agent writes over MCP: text $ deciduous remote status local server nodes 1 2 Only on the server (1) observation 96096527 "MCP probe obs" Differs: deciduous remote pull takes the server's side. $ deciduous remote pull Pulled: my-app /mcp. | Response | Meaning | | --- | --- | | 401 {"error":"unauthorized"} | No Authorization: Bearer header, or the wrong token. | | 404 with "message":"Session not found" and "detail":"This session expired or the server restarted. Send a new initialize request without a session id to start another." | The session id is unknown: the server restarted, the session idled out, or the client never sent notifications/initialized after initialize (a session that skips it is dropped, and the next call gets this). Reconnect the MCP server in the client. | | 405 on GET /mcp | Expected. The server offers no server-to-client stream; everything is POST. | | query_nodes has no argument "bogus". Its arguments are: branch, file, limit, search, status, type, workspace | Every tool refuses an argument it does not have and names the ones it does. Usually an agent using a stdio tool name or argument against the HTTP server; see MCP tools. | | node_id is not a node id: "11111111" | Server tools take the full server UUID (id in every result). The CLI's 8-character change_id prefixes do not work over MCP. | Reporting a problem Include deciduous --version, the server version (serverInfo.version in the MCP initialize reply), the command, and the error text as printed. Replace tokens with . deciduous remote watch --url prints a URL with the token in its query string; never paste that.

title: Graph concepts
label: Graph concepts
text: Graph concepts A deciduous graph is typed nodes joined by typed, directed edges, kept per workspace (one per repository) on a shared server. Seven node types, seven edge types, six statuses, and a confidence from 0 to 100. Every node has two identities: a server UUID that MCP tools use, and a change_id that survives every copy and every machine. The CLI and the server reject anything outside these lists, by name. Node types | Type | Records | | --- | --- | | goal | What someone asked for. Carries the request verbatim in prompt. The only node that may have no parent. | | option | One way to do it, considered before choosing. | | decision | The choice between options. A useful title names what it beat. | | action | Code or config changed to carry out a decision. | | outcome | What happened: the test count, the error, the number. | | observation | A fact learned along the way that matters to the plan. Attaches anywhere. | | revisit | An earlier choice being reconsidered: links the old decision, the observation that undid it, and the new decision. | The intended flow is goal -> option -> decision -> action -> outcome, with observations attached where they were learned. The graph does not enforce that order; find_orphans (MCP) reports any non-goal node with no incoming edge, which is the usual sign of a missing link. deciduous add --help lists six types and leaves out revisit; deciduous add revisit "..." works. Anything else is refused: text Error: unknown node type 'bogus'; expected one of: goal, decision, option, action, outcome, observation, revisit The server's query_nodes also accepts feedback, a legacy type kept so old imported graphs stay readable. New nodes cannot be created with it. Edge types An edge runs from one node to another in the same workspace. The two may be on different branches. | Type | From -> to | | --- | --- | | leads_to | The default: parent to child along the flow. | | chosen | Decision to the option it took. | | rejected | Decision to an option it turned down. | | requires | A node to something it depends on. | | blocks | A node to something it prevents. | | enables | A node to something it makes possible. | | took_from | The node an idea came from, to the node that reused it. Usually across branches, between agents. | log_decision draws chosen and rejected edges from the decision to its options; log_observation with took_from draws the edge from the source to the new observation. From the CLI: deciduous link -t took_from -r "why". Status pending (the default), active, completed, rejected, superseded, abandoned. deciduous status --help lists only the first four; all six are accepted: text $ deciduous status 1 done Error: unknown status 'done'; expected one of: pending, active, completed, rejected, superseded, abandoned superseded is for a decision that was right once and has been replaced (deciduous archaeology supersede sets it, with --cascade for descendants); abandoned is for something tried and dropped. Both keep the node, which is the point: the graph is most useful about the paths not taken. Deleting a node (deciduous delete, MCP delete_node) is a soft delete on the server. Confidence An integer from 0 to 100, set by whoever wrote the node. It is a judgement, not a measurement. The CLI refuses anything outside the range: text error: invalid value '150' for '--confidence ': 150 is not in 0..=100 Identity: id, change_id, local number | Identity | Looks like | Where it works | | --- | --- | --- | | Server id | 8889e255-4305-4fc5-a4f2-d316db4e316e | Every MCP tool that takes node_id, parent_id, from_node_id, to_node_id. The CLI accepts it too. | | change_id | 96096527-2046-4a39-863a-7e67c3cf194e | The same on every machine, in graph.json, and on the server. The CLI accepts a prefix (deciduous link 5e906850 96096527); deciduous nodes prints the first 8 characters in the CHANGE column. Over MCP, log_observation's took_from and related_to accept a full change_id; show_node does not. | | Local number | 1, 2, 3 | One machine's database only. Two machines number the same node differently. | MCP tools do not accept prefixes: show_node with "11111111" answers node_id is not a node id: "11111111". A change_id also makes a write safe to retry. add_node with a change_id the workspace already holds, for a node of the same type and title, returns that node with created: false instead of making a second one. The same change_id with a different title is refused: text change_id 11111111-2222-4333-8444-555555555555 is already node 3bcdac84-4e0d-410f-890f-d1f8f32712a4, action "idempotent"; this call names a action "different". Nothing was written. Use another change_id, or update_node to change that node. Workspace A workspace is one repository's graph on a server. Its name comes from workspace under [remote] in .deciduous/config.toml, which remote init and remote setup write: by default the repository's root directory name, lowercased (Docs_Ref_Upper becomes docs_ref_upper), or whatever --workspace says. The server trims and lowercases names and refuses anything that looks like a path. The first repository to write to a workspace claims it by its root commit ids. Clones and worktrees of that repository share the root commit and are let in; an unrelated repository with the same directory name is refused until it picks another name or names this one explicitly (see Troubleshooting). Over MCP, the workspace for a call is decided in this order: the X-Deciduous-Workspace header if the client sends one, then the call's workspace argument, then scratch. Read tools also accept workspace: "" for every workspace at once; writes refuse it. A workspace is a name for routing, not a permission: anyone holding the server's token can read and write all of them. See Architecture. Branch Every node records the git branch it was written on, in its metadata. The CLI detects it (--branch overrides, --no-branch skips); MCP clients pass branch on each write, because the server cannot see the agent's checkout. Branch is for filtering (deciduous nodes -b feature-x, query_nodes with branch) and for check_activity's view of who is writing where. Nothing is locked by branch: two agents on one branch both write, and their nodes interleave.

title: CLI reference
label: CLI reference
text: CLI reference The deciduous commands people actually use, grouped by what you are trying to do, with flags as deciduous --help prints them in 1.1.0. In a project with a [remote], every write command writes the local database, queues an op in .deciduous/remote-log.jsonl, and sends it to the server before it exits; every read command reads the local database, which is a cache refreshed by remote pull. Commands marked server need a [remote]; commands marked no server only matter without one. Anywhere a command takes a node, it accepts a local number, a change_id prefix, or a server UUID. Connect a project to a server remote setup (server) Connect this project to a shared graph server, step by step. In a terminal it asks; flags answer for scripts. Ends by writing [remote], storing the token if needed, and registering Claude Code (only if Claude Code has no deciduous server yet). | Flag | Meaning | | --- | --- | | --url | Use the server at this URL (token from DECIDUOUS_MCP_TOKEN or the stored one). The usual choice. | | --local | Use this machine's server; set it up if there is none. See Without a shared server. | | --port | Port for this machine's server, first setup only. | | --database-url | PostgreSQL for this machine's server; ?sslmode=require\|verify-ca\|verify-full for TLS. The environment's DATABASE_URL is never used unless passed here. | | --docker | Run this machine's server in Docker. | | --docker-postgres | Also run a new PostgreSQL in Docker (implies --docker). | text $ DECIDUOUS_MCP_TOKEN= deciduous remote setup --url https://deciduous.example.com A token given only through the environment is checked but not stored. remote login / remote logout login [--url ] reads a token from stdin and stores it in ~/.config/deciduous/credentials (mode 0600; $XDG_CONFIG_HOME/deciduous/credentials if that is set). With --url it checks the token against that server first and stores nothing if the server refuses it. logout deletes the stored token. There is one stored token per machine; see One token per machine. remote init (server) Point this project at a server without the wizard: checks /health and the token, claims the workspace for this repository, sends any local history the server lacks, writes [remote]. Does not touch Claude Code. | Flag | Meaning | | --- | --- | | --workspace | Workspace name. Defaults to the git repository's root directory name. Naming an existing workspace explicitly lets this repository share it. | text $ deciduous remote init http://127.0.0.1:4000 --workspace my-app Remote: http://127.0.0.1:4000 workspace: my-app claim: claimed (by this repository's root commit) server holds 0 nodes, 0 edges, 0 documents Written to .deciduous/config.toml. The token stays in ~/.config/deciduous/credentials (or DECIDUOUS_MCP_TOKEN), never here. remote adopt [ROOT] --url (server) Walk a directory for projects that already have a .deciduous and point each at the server. Existing configuration is left alone. -n, --dry-run shows what would change. Check and repair the connection remote status (server) How far the local copy has drifted from the server: ops waiting and rejected, node and edge counts, and every row that differs, field by field. Exits 0 only on In sync. text Remote: http://127.0.0.1:4000 Workspace: my-app Log: 0 write(s) waiting, 0 rejected (/home/you/code/my-app/.deciduous/remote-log.jsonl) local server nodes 2 2 edges 1 1 In sync: no writes waiting, and every node, edge and document matches field by field. Themes and tags are not sent to the server, so they are not compared. remote push (server) Send the ops waiting in .deciduous/remote-log.jsonl, in order. The server applies each at most once, so pushing twice is safe. Normally unnecessary: every write sends what is waiting. | Flag | Meaning | | --- | --- | | --retry-rejected | Send rejected ops again, after fixing the cause. | | --drop-rejected | Discard the ops the server rejected (read why with remote status first). | | --drop | Discard one op, waiting or rejected, by the start of its id. | | --seed | Also send nodes, edges and documents the server lacks that no op covers. Never changes a row the server has. | | --repair | Also send what this copy changed and never logged, for nodes status lists as Different, field by field where the server has not changed the field since the last pull. | | --overwrite-server | With --repair: also send fields the server did change, over the server's value. | | --overwrite | Replace the server's copy of every row with the local one (the pre-1.0.3 behaviour). Last resort. | DECIDUOUS_OPS_TIMEOUT= changes the 120-second limit per request. remote pull (server) Refresh the local database from the server: takes the server's side of every difference. Run it before reading with nodes, show or serve if agents have been writing over MCP. No flags. remote watch (server) Stream this workspace's writes, one line per node event, reconnecting with backoff. text $ deciduous remote watch Watching: my-app 13:38:02 main outcome "watched outcome" | Flag | Meaning | | --- | --- | | --types | Only these node types, comma-separated. | | --branch | Only this branch; repeat for several. | | --edges | Also show edge events. | | --json | Raw JSON frame per event. | | --url | Print the socket URL and exit. The URL carries the token in its query string. | | --claude-code | Print the URL plus a ready-to-paste Monitor tool call for Claude Code, and exit. Also carries the token. | Record decisions add Types: goal, option, decision, action, outcome, observation, revisit (--help omits revisit; it works). | Flag | Meaning | | --- | --- | | -d, --description | Description. Observations warn without one. | | -c, --confidence | Confidence. | | -p, --prompt | The user's request, verbatim. Warns when it looks like a summary. | | --prompt-stdin | Read the prompt from stdin, for multi-line requests. | | -f, --files | Associated files, comma-separated. | | -b, --branch / --no-branch | Override or skip branch detection. | | --commit | HEAD, a branch, a tag, a hash or prefix. Stored as the full hash; a rev git cannot resolve is refused. | | --date | Backdate: RFC 3339, YYYY-MM-DD or YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM:SS. | bash deciduous add goal "Bound the retry delay" -c 90 --prompt-stdin / unlink link -r, --rationale , -t, --edge-type (default leads_to; also requires, chosen, rejected, blocks, enables, took_from). unlink -t, --type removes only the edge of that type, required when two nodes are joined by more than one. status pending, active, completed, rejected, superseded, abandoned. (--help lists the first four.) prompt [PROMPT] Set or replace a node's prompt; reads stdin when the text is omitted. delete Delete a node and its edges. --dry-run shows what would go. Read the graph | Command | Flags | | --- | --- | | nodes | -b, --branch, -t, --node-type, --theme | | edges | none | | show | --json | | graph | none; the whole graph as JSON on stdout | | pulse | -b, --branch, -r, --recent (default 10), --json, --summary. Active state, gaps, health. | | serve | -p, --port (default 3000). The web viewer, on the local database. | | commands | -l, --limit (default 20). Recent CLI writes with exit status. | All of these read the local database. Over MCP, agents read the server directly; see MCP tools. Design history | Command | Purpose and flags | | --- | --- | | archaeology pivot | Creates observation -> revisit -> new decision and marks the old one superseded, in one step. -c, --confidence, -r, --reason, --dry-run. | | archaeology supersede | Mark superseded. --cascade for every descendant, --dry-run. | | archaeology timeline | Nodes in time order. -l, --limit (0 = all), -t, --node-type, -b, --branch, --json. | | narratives init / show / pivots | .deciduous/narratives.md: seed it from active goals (-o, --force), print it (-p), list revisit chains (-b, --json). | See Design history. Evidence | Command | Purpose and flags | | --- | --- | | doc attach | Attach a file. -d, --description, --ai-describe (uses the claude CLI). | | doc list [NODE_ID] | --include-detached, --json. | | doc show / doc open | Details (--json) / open in the default application. | | doc describe [TEXT] | Set the description; stdin if omitted; --ai. | | doc detach | Soft-delete. doc gc [--dry-run] removes files nothing references. | | transcript list | This project's Claude Code sessions and whether each is imported. --dir, --json. | | transcript import ... | Derive goals, actions and outcomes from a transcript, each with evidence. Re-importing adds nothing. --dry-run, --no-hash, --json. | See Documents and transcripts. title: MCP tools
label: MCP tools
text: MCP tools There are two MCP servers with different tool sets, and an agent gets whichever one its client is configured for. The graph server answers at /mcp over HTTP with 21 tools and writes PostgreSQL directly; this is what remote setup registers with Claude Code and what this page is mostly about. deciduous mcp is a stdio server with 34 tools under different names. It writes the local database, and in a project with a [remote] those writes go on to the server through the CLI's op log, exactly like deciduous add. Nothing configures it for you, and it does not send the server's logging instructions. The two lists below are from tools/list against deciduous 1.1.0 on 2026-11-08. Which one an agent has | | Graph server ( /mcp) | deciduous mcp (stdio) | | --- | --- | --- | | Transport | Streamable HTTP, Authorization: Bearer | stdin/stdout, a process per session | | Configured by | remote setup (Claude Code, user scope, if none is registered), or by hand: Connect your agents | you, in the client: {"command": "deciduous", "args": ["mcp"]} | | Writes go to | PostgreSQL, at once, visible to every agent | the local database; in a project with a [remote], also queued in .deciduous/remote-log.jsonl and sent to the server, as CLI writes are. Without a [remote], they stay local. | | Reads come from | the server | the local database, which is a cache: it shows what other agents wrote only after deciduous remote pull | | Tools | 21 | 34 | | initialize reply | serverInfo {name: deciduous-mcp, version} plus instructions (the logging rules agents follow) | serverInfo {name: deciduous, version}, no instructions | Use the graph server for agents. The stdio server is for a project with no server at all (Without a shared server) or for the local-only tools it has that the graph server lacks (themes, DOT export, writeups, sessions). A stdio write in a project with a [remote] was checked: add_node over deciduous mcp returned Created observation node 3, and deciduous remote status then said In sync with the server holding the node. Talking to the graph server by hand An MCP client does this for you. With curl, the sequence is: initialize without a session id, read mcp-session-id from the response headers, send notifications/initialized with that id, then make calls with it. Accept must list both application/json and text/event-stream. bash BASE=https://deciduous.example.com H=(-H "Authorization: Bearer $DECIDUOUS_MCP_TOKEN" -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -H 'Accept: application/json, text/event-stream') curl -s -D headers.txt -X POST "$BASE/mcp" "${H[@]}" -d '{"jsonrpc":"2.0","id":1,"method":"initialize", "params":{"protocolVersion":"2025-06-18","capabilities":{},"clientInfo":{"name":"probe","version":"0"}}}' SID=$(grep -i '^mcp-session-id' headers.txt | awk '{print $2}' | tr -d '\r') curl -s -X POST "$BASE/mcp" "${H[@]}" -H "mcp-session-id: $SID" \ -d '{"jsonrpc":"2.0","method":"notifications/initialized"}' curl -s -X POST "$BASE/mcp" "${H[@]}" -H "mcp-session-id: $SID" \ -d '{"jsonrpc":"2.0","id":2,"method":"tools/list"}' Skip notifications/initialized and the session is dropped: the next call gets HTTP 404 Session not found with This session expired or the server restarted. Send a new initialize request without a session id to start another. The same reply follows a server restart. GET /mcp answers 405; there is no server-to-client stream. Tool results come back as JSON text inside result.content[0].text. A tool error is a JSON-RPC error whose message says what was wrong, including any argument the tool does not have: text query_nodes has no argument "bogus". Its arguments are: branch, file, limit, search, status, type, workspace Workspace and branch on every call Every tool except list_workspaces takes workspace. The server decides which workspace a call acts on in this order: 1. The X-Deciduous-Workspace header, if the client sends one (a repository's .mcp.json can). It wins over the argument: an add_node sent with "workspace": "elsewhere-xyz" on a connection pinned to my-app landed in my-app. 2. The workspace argument: the workspace under [remote] in .deciduous/config.toml, which is what the CLI uses. 3. scratch. Read tools accept "workspace": "" for all workspaces at once, unless the connection is pinned; writes refuse it. A read naming a workspace that does not exist is an error; the first write creates it. Pass branch on every write. The server cannot see the agent's checkout, and check_activity shows writers by branch. Nothing is locked: since 1.0.8 there are no branch leases, and two sessions writing one branch both succeed. The 21 graph-server tools Required arguments in bold. Node ids are full server UUIDs (the id in every result); prefixes are refused. Write | Tool | Arguments | Notes | | --- | --- | --- | | add_node | node_type, title, description, status, confidence, prompt, files, commit, branch, parent_id, edge_type, rationale, change_id | parent_id creates and links in one transaction (edge_type, rationale apply to that edge). A non-goal node without a parent comes back with suggested_parents, never linked for you. A repeated change_id returns the existing node with created: false. | | add_edge | from_node_id, to_node_id, edge_type, rationale, branch | For took_from, from is the node the idea came from. Never in the same batch as the add_node whose id it needs. | | update_node | node_id, title, description, status, metadata, branch | metadata is merged: keys sent are set, a key sent as null is removed, others are kept. | | delete_node | node_id, branch | Soft delete. | | delete_edge | from_node_id, to_node_id, edge_type, branch | edge_type defaults to leads_to. | | log_observation | title, description, related_to, took_from, why, tags, branch | related_to and took_from take a UUID or a full change_id. why becomes the took_from edge's rationale. | | log_decision | title, chosen_option, rejected_options, rationale, parent_node_id, confidence, branch | One transaction: decision, options, chosen/rejected edges. Options are objects or plain titles. | | capture_conversation_turn | summary, goal, observations, options_considered, decision, action, outcome, parent_node_id, confidence, branch | One step's nodes and edges, all or nothing. parent_node_id hangs it under the goal in progress. | | close_thread | title, description, parent_node_id, goal_node_id, success, lessons_learned, next_steps, branch | Writes the outcome; goal_node_id marks the goal completed; lessons become observations, next steps become goals. | Read | Tool | Arguments | Notes | | --- | --- | --- | | list_workspaces | none | Every workspace with node and edge counts. | | check_activity | branches (default 20) | Who wrote to this workspace in the last five minutes (branch, client, whether it is you), and the newest node on each branch. Call before a burst of writes. | | query_nodes | type, status, branch, search, file, limit (default 100) | file matches metadata.files. type also accepts legacy feedback, status legacy done. | | show_node | node_id | The node, its edges, documents, themes, and up to 10 related nodes sharing a file or commit. Takes a UUID, not a change_id. | | get_graph | branch, include_details, max_nodes (default 2000) | Refuses a larger graph rather than truncating. | | get_ancestors / get_descendants | node_id, max_depth (default 50), max_nodes (default 1000) | Walk edges backward / forward. | | find_orphans | suggest_parents | Non-goal nodes with no incoming edge; with suggest_parents, ranked guesses for the first 25. | | ask_graph | question, scope (all, active, decisions, goals, observations, recent), include_context (default true) | Text search (trigram and full text), then follows the edges the question implies. Says how each result was reached, and stops early when a distinctive word in the question matches nothing. Not a language model. | | consolidation_report | similarity (0.6), stale_days (14), max_nodes, max_pairs, max_items | Proposes merges, missing revisits, stale actions and parents. Changes nothing. | Message board | Tool | Arguments | | --- | --- | | post_message | author, subject, body, reply_to, branch | | read_messages | unanswered_for, to, author, branch, query, since_id, id, limit (default 50) | Messages are per workspace and are not graph nodes. See Many agents, one graph. The 34 stdio tools deciduous mcp exposes: add_node, attach_document, create_theme, delete_node, end_session, export_dot, find_orphans, generate_writeup, get_branch_summary, get_graph, get_node_context, get_pulse, get_session, get_timeline, link_nodes, list_documents, list_edges, list_nodes, list_sessions, list_themes, post_message, read_messages, resume_session, search_nodes, show_node, start_session, sync, sync_status, tag_node, trace_chain, unlink_nodes, untag_node, update_prompt, update_status. Where a name matches a graph-server tool, the arguments and ids still differ: stdio tools take local node numbers (Created observation node 3), the graph server takes UUIDs. Where the job matches, the name differs: link_nodes vs add_edge, list_nodes/search_nodes vs query_nodes, update_status vs update_node. An agent moved from one server to the other with instructions written for the first will hit has no argument and unknown-tool errors; For agents is written for the graph server.

title: Architecture and trust
label: Architecture and trust
text: Architecture and trust The graph lives in PostgreSQL behind one server process. Agents reach that server over HTTPS MCP; the CLI reaches the same server, over the same HTTPS and token, through ordinary JSON endpoints (/ops, /export, /events) rather than MCP, sending each write from a local log of operations. Each developer's .deciduous/deciduous.db is a cache of the server's copy, not a second source of truth. One bearer token opens the whole server: every workspace, read and write. What runs where text developer machine the server's host ┌───────────────────────────────┐ ┌──────────────────────────────┐ │ agent (Claude Code, ...) ────┼── POST /mcp ─────►│ deciduous-mcp (Elixir) │ │ │ Bearer │ /mcp /ops /export │ │ deciduous CLI │ │ /events /blob /documents │ │ .deciduous/deciduous.db │── POST /ops ─────►│ /health /ready │ │ (cache) │◄─ GET /export ────│ │ │ .deciduous/remote-log.jsonl │ │ │ │ │ (writes not yet sent) │◄─ WS /events ─────│ ▼ │ └───────────────────────────────┘ │ PostgreSQL: every │ │ workspace's nodes, edges, │ │ documents, messages │ └──────────────────────────────┘ | Piece | Where | What it holds | | --- | --- | --- | | deciduous-mcp | A VM behind a TLS proxy (Run a server), or this machine (Without a shared server) | Nothing durable. Speaks MCP at /mcp, applies CLI ops at /ops, serves exports, documents and the event socket. | | PostgreSQL | Next to the server, or managed | Every workspace: nodes, edges, document bytes, board messages, workspace claims, write activity. Back this up; it is the graph. | | .deciduous/deciduous.db | Each clone | A cache of one workspace, plus themes, tags and the local command log, which the server does not have. | | .deciduous/remote-log.jsonl | Each clone, next to the cache, ignored by git | CLI writes the server has not acknowledged. | | .deciduous/config.toml | Each clone, committed | [remote] url and workspace. Never a token. | | ~/.config/deciduous/credentials | Each machine | The one stored token. | The server's HTTP routes: /health (unauthenticated, process liveness), /ready (database and migrations), /mcp, /ops, /export, /import, /claim, /locate, PUT /blob/:hash, /documents/:id, /messages, /events. Everything except /health requires the token. Two write paths, one store An agent's MCP write is a transaction in PostgreSQL. When the tool returns, every other agent can read it. A CLI write (deciduous add, link, status, and deciduous mcp over stdio in a project with a [remote]) goes through three steps: 1. The write and an op describing it commit together in the local database (the op sits in a remote_outbox table), so a crash cannot keep one without the other. 2. The op is appended to .deciduous/remote-log.jsonl. An op names only what changed: {"kind":"update_node","change_id":"…","set":{"status":"completed"}}, not the whole node. 3. Before the command exits, the waiting ops are sent to POST /ops, with a 10-second budget. The server applies each op at most once, by op_id, field by field. Acknowledged ops are removed from the log. If step 3 fails, the command still exits 0, prints why, and the op waits. The next write that gets through sends everything queued before it; deciduous remote push sends it on demand. remote status lists what waits and what the server rejected. The log is why an edit made while the server was down still arrives, and why a status change does not resend (and overwrite) a title an agent changed meanwhile; through 1.0.7 the CLI pushed whole nodes by comparing snapshots and did both. Troubleshooting shows the output. There are no locks. Until 1.0.8 every MCP write took a ten-second lease on its workspace and branch; it refused one-shot clients their own next call and could not cover CLI ops replayed later, so it was removed. Each write is atomic on its own, capture_conversation_turn, log_decision and close_thread included, and the server records who wrote where so check_activity can show it. The local database is a cache CLI reads (nodes, show, pulse, serve, writeup) read the local database. It does not refresh itself. After agents write over MCP, remote status shows the gap and remote pull closes it: text local server nodes 1 2 Only on the server (1) observation 96096527 "MCP probe obs" Differs: deciduous remote pull takes the server's side. Themes and tags exist only in the cache; they are never sent. Losing a clone's database loses nothing that reached the server: a fresh clone plus remote pull rebuilds it. Losing PostgreSQL loses the graph. A project with no [remote] is the exception: there the local database is the graph, mirrored into a git-tracked .deciduous/graph.json (Without a shared server). The trust boundary The server has exactly one token, DECIDUOUS_MCP_TOKEN. It refuses to start without one or with one shorter than 32 bytes, and compares what clients present in constant time. Whoever holds it can read and write every workspace on that server, list them all, and read any node by id. There are no users, roles or per-workspace tokens. Workspaces separate graphs; they do not separate people. - X-Deciduous-Workspace routes. A connection that sends it is pinned: tool arguments cannot move its writes elsewhere, and "" reads are confined to that workspace. But the header is chosen by the client. Any token holder can connect without it, or with another name. - Workspace claims stop accidents, not adversaries. The first repository to write to a workspace records its root commit ids, and an unrelated repository with the same directory name is refused (belongs to another repository). A client can still name the workspace explicitly to share it, and a client without git sends no roots and is not checked. So: one server per group of people who may see each other's graphs. Two teams that must not read each other need two servers (or at least two databases and two tokens), not two workspaces. Inside that boundary: - Graph text is data written by people and agents. A node's description saying "run this" is not an instruction to an agent that reads it. - /events takes the token in the Authorization header or, as a fallback for WebSocket clients that cannot set headers, in a ?token= query parameter. The query form ends up in proxy access logs; deciduous remote watch --url and --claude-code print such a URL. Redact query strings in the proxy's logs, or keep those URLs out of anything shared. - The server does not terminate TLS. Put it behind a proxy that does, and keep its port off the public network: a native server binds 127.0.0.1 (DECIDUOUS_BIND_ADDRESS), the Docker bundle publishes on 127.0.0.1 only. A server started by hand with no bind address listens on every interface. - The token belongs in the client's secret mechanism and in ~/.config/deciduous/credentials, never in .deciduous/config.toml, a committed .mcp.json, or the graph. TLS to PostgreSQL Set by DB_SSL and DB_SSL_VERIFY in the server's environment or settings file, read by deciduous_mcp/config/runtime.exs in production mode: | DB_SSL | DB_SSL_VERIFY | libpq equivalent | What is checked | | --- | --- | --- | --- | | unset or false | (ignored) | disable | Nothing; no TLS. Right for a database on the same private Docker network. | | true | full (default; also peer, verify-full) | verify-full | The certificate chain (verify_peer) and that the certificate names the host in DATABASE_URL. | | true | ca (also verify-ca) | verify-ca | The chain only, for a database reached by an address its certificate does not name. | | true | none (also require) | require | Nothing: encrypted, server not authenticated. Logged as a warning at every boot. | The chain is checked against the system CA store, or against DB_SSL_CA_FILE (a PEM file) for a private CA. A missing or empty CA file stops the server at boot instead of failing every connection later. Each boot logs the mode in effect; this machine's native server, on a local PostgreSQL, logs Database TLS: off (DB_SSL unset or false). Earlier versions of these docs said the server used verify_none whenever DB_SSL=true. That was true of 1.0.1 only. Since then, true alone means full verification, and unverified TLS has to be asked for by name. A 1.0.1 deployment upgrading with a private CA needs DB_SSL_CA_FILE; one whose certificate does not name the address it connects to needs DB_SSL_VERIFY=ca. Source map | Path | What is there | | --- | --- | | deciduous_mcp/lib/deciduous_mcp/web/router.ex | Every HTTP route | | deciduous_mcp/lib/deciduous_mcp/web/auth.ex, workspace_plug.ex | The token check; the workspace pin | | deciduous_mcp/lib/deciduous_mcp/mcp/scope.ex | How a call's workspace is decided | | deciduous_mcp/lib/deciduous_mcp/mcp/tools/ | The 21 tools | | deciduous_mcp/lib/deciduous_mcp/activity.ex | Write activity, and why the branch lock went | | deciduous_mcp/lib/deciduous_mcp/graph/workspaces.ex | Workspace claims by root commit | | deciduous_mcp/config/runtime.exs | Every setting the server reads, including database TLS | | src/oplog.rs | The op log: format, crash safety, compaction | | src/remote.rs | remote , token lookup, status and pull | | src/server.rs, src/local_server.rs | remote setup and this machine's server | | src/records.rs | graph.json and the merge driver, for projects with no server | | src/mcp/ | The stdio MCP server |

title: Develop deciduous
label: Develop deciduous
text: Develop deciduous The repository holds three things that are built and tested separately: the Rust CLI at the root (cargo), the graph server in deciduous_mcp/ (Elixir, mix), and two web builds, the graph viewer in web/ and this documentation site in scripts/docs/. A change to a tool's behaviour usually needs both the Rust and the Elixir side: the CLI's deciduous mcp and the server's /mcp are separate implementations with different tool sets (MCP tools). The CLI The toolchain is pinned in rust-toolchain.toml to 1.92.0, with clippy and rustfmt; rustup picks it up from the file. Stable is pinned on purpose: a newer clippy reported 29 errors on an unchanged tree once. text $ cargo build Compiling deciduous v1.1.0 (/Users/you/code/deciduous) Finished dev profile [unoptimized + debuginfo] target(s) in 8.36s (an incremental build; a clean one takes minutes). Before committing, the repository's own rules ask for all three: bash cargo test cargo clippy --all-targets cargo build --release Use ./target/debug/deciduous or ./target/release/deciduous when checking a change. The deciduous on your PATH is whatever you installed, and it will happily answer instead. cargo test on a Mac with Homebrew tests/git_sync_integration.rs drives real git with the freshly built binary as the merge driver. It builds the PATH for each simulated developer from the directory holding git, and refuses to run if that directory also holds an installed deciduous, which would stand in for the binary under test. With Homebrew's git and Homebrew's deciduous both in /opt/homebrew/bin, every test in that file fails at once: text thread 'a_merge_whose_ancestor_will_not_parse_is_refused_not_decided_by_timestamp' panicked at tests/git_sync_integration.rs:43:5: git shares a directory with an installed deciduous (/opt/homebrew/bin) That is the test protecting itself, not a bug. Put the system git first: bash PATH=/usr/bin:$PATH cargo test text $ PATH=/usr/bin:$PATH cargo test --test git_sync_integration a_merge_whose_ancestor test a_merge_whose_ancestor_will_not_parse_is_refused_not_decided_by_timestamp ... ok test result: ok. 1 passed; 0 failed; 0 ignored; 0 measured; 23 filtered out; finished in 3.09s The full suite run that way passed 687 tests on 2026-11-08. It is slow; filter by test binary (--test ) or name while iterating. Tests that run deciduous init in a temporary directory need DECIDUOUS_NO_SERVER=1, or init stops at the server step (Troubleshooting). Templates deciduous init and update write files from templates in src/init/. src/init/known_templates.rs is generated: the sha256 of every template ever shipped, which is how update tells a file deciduous wrote from one a user edited. It is built from every template text in the repository's git history, so regenerate it after a template change is committed: python3 scripts/gen_known_templates.py > src/init/known_templates.rs. A template text missing from the list is one update will treat as the user's and keep. The graph server deciduous_mcp/ is an Elixir application (mix.exs declares Elixir ~> 1.16; CI uses Elixir 1.18.4 on OTP 28.3.3). It refuses to boot without a DECIDUOUS_MCP_TOKEN of at least 32 bytes, tests included. mix test creates and migrates its database first (the test alias), using PGHOST, PGUSER, PGPASSWORD (default postgres/postgres on localhost) and database deciduous_mcp_test. CI's job, in .github/workflows/integration.yml: bash cd deciduous_mcp export MIX_ENV=test PGHOST=localhost PGUSER=postgres PGPASSWORD=postgres export DECIDUOUS_MCP_TOKEN=mix-test-token-not-a-secret-0000000000000000 mix deps.get mix test against a postgres:17-alpine service. Development (config/dev.exs) uses deciduous_mcp_dev with the same credentials. Neither was run for this page. Things that are easy to get wrong here: - A new tool lives in lib/deciduous_mcp/mcp/tools/ and has to be registered with the server to appear in tools/list. Check the live list after a rebuild; the CLI's tools are a different list. - Every tool's workspace argument is merged in by DeciduousMcp.MCP.Scope; resolve reads and writes through it so the X-Deciduous-Workspace pin is honoured. - Unknown arguments are refused by name. A new argument has to be in the schema or clients get has no argument. - A migration needs STRUCTURE.sql regenerated with it (scripts/dump_structure.sh against a disposable PostgreSQL 17). CI's structure job fails when they disagree. - Server dependencies are audited at release: mix hex.audit must be clean or the self-contained server build fails. Release executables are built with Burrito (Dockerfile.burrito, BURRITO_TARGET=darwin_arm64 mix release, output in burrito_out/). To try an unreleased server through the CLI's own installer, point DECIDUOUS_SERVER_BINARY at that file (or DECIDUOUS_SERVER_BUNDLE at a Docker bundle) before remote setup --local. That installs a service on your machine; do it on a machine where that is what you want. deciduous_mcp/DEPLOY.md documents every server setting. The web viewer web/ is React and TypeScript in one App.tsx, built by Vite into a single HTML file that the CLI embeds. After changing anything under web/src/: bash cd web && npm run build && cd .. cp web/dist/index.html src/viewer.html cp web/dist/index.html docs/demo/index.html cargo test cargo build --release deciduous serve then serves the new viewer from the rebuilt binary. npm run typecheck and npm test (Vitest) run in web/. scripts/validate-types.sh checks that the TypeScript types in web/src/types/ still match the Rust ones. These steps are from the repository's CLAUDE.md and web/package.json; they were not run for this page. This documentation The site is generated from docs/content/.md by scripts/docs/. Navigation and labels are in scripts/docs/pages.json; each page needs exactly one H1, and its first paragraph becomes the page description. Links between pages are relative (Architecture). bash npm ci --prefix scripts/docs npm run build --prefix scripts/docs writes the HTML npm run check --prefix scripts/docs verifies generated files match, then runs test.mjs Generated HTML and the search index are committed with the Markdown; CI fails if they disagree. To look at it: python3 -m http.server 8766 --directory docs --bind 127.0.0.1. Releasing The steps (both version numbers, both changelogs, mix hex.audit, tagging by hand from the merge commit, and watching release.yml until crates.io and the Homebrew tap show the version) are in the repository's CLAUDE.md under "Release Process". A release that looks finished may have published nothing; check gh release view vX.Y.Z, crates.io and the tap.
